A brain-wave test (EEG) and a visit to the nerve specialists, in case it was a seizure
Tell the family that fainting is common in teenagers, and send him home
0.fix: Get the heart tracing and the ultrasound

terms.meaning: Moving pictures of the heart made with sound waves. It shows how thick the walls are and how blood flows through.
A reflex that briefly drops the blood pressure. It usually happens while standing still, after a warning of warmth, sweating or nausea.
A test that tilts a patient upright, while they are watched, to bring on a faint. It is for cases where the cause is unclear.

outcomes.story: He starts on the treadmill with a tracing running. A few minutes in, as the slope steepens, he turns pale and says the room is going gray. His blood pressure has fallen when it should be climbing. The test is stopped and he is laid flat. He feels normal again within a minute.
outcomes.reply: Exercise is what made him black out yesterday, and we have not looked at his heart yet. An exercise test can be useful later, at a heart center, with the right team watching. Not today. Now we get the tracing and the ultrasound.
outcomes.alarm: Nearly passed out on the treadmill · blood pressure fell with exercise

outcomes.story: The tracing takes a few minutes. The ultrasound is done down the hall, and he lies still for it. The reports go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. When a young athlete blacks out during exercise, you look at the heart first: its electrical pattern and its structure. Everything else waits.

outcomes.story: You request a tilt-table test. The resident sets the form aside.
outcomes.reply: A tilt test is for repeated faints once the heart has been cleared. A simple faint comes on while standing still, with a warning. He went down mid-sprint with none. The heart comes first.

outcomes.story: You start the referral for a brain-wave test. The resident reads it over your shoulder.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here looks like a seizure. He had no warning feeling and no bitten tongue, and he woke clear-headed. A blackout during hard exercise points to the heart.

outcomes.story: You begin to tell his mother it was a simple faint. The resident steps in before she picks up her bag.
outcomes.reply: This is the one kind of faint we never wave through. A blackout during exercise with no warning, a murmur, and a relative who died suddenly at 38: each is a red flag for a dangerous heart condition. He does not leave without a heart check.

3.resident: The ultrasound shows a very thick heart wall that partly blocks the way out with every beat. The blockage gets worse when his heart is less full.
3.question: What is the plan now?
options: Start lisinopril, to relax his arteries and shrink the muscle
Start furosemide, a water tablet, to lower the pressure across the blockage
Start verapamil, with nitroglycerin under the tongue for chest tightness
Start a beta-blocker, and send him urgently to heart specialists to be assessed for an implanted defibrillator
3.fix: Start a beta-blocker and refer him

terms.meaning: A medicine that slows the heart and softens each beat. A slower heart has longer to fill, and a fuller heart is less blocked.
A small device under the skin that watches the heart’s rhythm and gives a shock if a deadly rhythm starts.
A medicine that relaxes blood vessels. Lisinopril and nitroglycerin are two.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for lisinopril. The resident reads it before it is printed.
outcomes.reply: Lisinopril relaxes the arteries. With less to push against, his heart empties faster and more completely, and the thick wall and the valve flap close in on each other. The blockage gets worse. And it has not been shown to shrink this kind of muscle.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for furosemide. The pharmacist calls the clinic before filling it.
outcomes.reply: A water tablet drains fluid, so his heart fills less. In this condition a less full heart is a more blocked heart. He needs to stay well filled, and well hydrated.

outcomes.story: You write for verapamil and nitroglycerin. The resident stops at the second line.
outcomes.reply: Nitroglycerin relaxes the veins, so less blood returns to the heart and the blockage tightens. It could make him black out. Verapamil has a place in this condition, but it is the second choice, for when a beta-blocker does not work or cannot be taken.

outcomes.story: You explain the medicine to him and his mother. The resident calls the heart center, and he is given an urgent appointment for a full risk assessment, including a monitor to wear and an MRI of his heart. He is told to stay well hydrated.
outcomes.reply: The beta-blocker eases the blockage. It does not protect him from a dangerous rhythm. That is what the specialists will weigh up, and why they will discuss a defibrillator with him and his family.

4.resident: One more conversation before they leave. This condition usually runs in families, and he wants to know about Friday’s game.
4.question: What do we tell them about sports and about his relatives?
options: He can keep playing if he drinks plenty of water and takes his beta-blocker
His relatives need checking only if they get symptoms
No hard competitive sport until the specialists have assessed him, and his parents and any brothers or sisters all need a heart check
No family checks are needed, because his uncle died of a heart attack
4.fix: Pause competitive sport and check the family

terms.meaning: Parents, brothers, sisters and children. This condition is usually passed on so that each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.
Checking people who feel well, here with a heart tracing and a heart ultrasound, to find a condition before it causes harm.
A choice made by the patient, the family and the specialists together, once the risks are understood.

outcomes.story: You start to tell him Friday’s game is fine. The resident cuts in.
outcomes.reply: Not yet. He blacked out during a sprint yesterday, and no one has sized up his risk. Some people with this condition do go back to sport, but that is decided with the specialists after a full assessment, not before it.

outcomes.story: You tell his mother the rest of the family can wait and see. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: In this condition the first symptom can be a sudden death. That is why relatives are checked while they feel well. Waiting for symptoms throws away the chance to protect them.

outcomes.story: You explain it to them both. He is unhappy about missing Friday’s game, and his mother has a lot of questions. She starts arranging heart checks for the family, beginning with his father.
outcomes.reply: That is the right message. Sitting out is a pause, not a verdict: the specialists will decide with him what he can return to. His father’s “thick heart walls” and his uncle’s death may well be the same condition, which makes the family checks urgent.

outcomes.story: You tell them the uncle’s heart attack is a separate matter. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A 38-year-old dying suddenly while swimming, with no autopsy, is how this condition often hides in a family. “Heart attack” was a guess. It makes checking the family more important, not less.

differential.resident: The heart tracing and the ultrasound are in his chart. Read them, then tell me what he has.
differential.question: What explains his blackout and his murmur?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction: an inherited thickening of the heart muscle that blocks the way out
Athlete’s heart: normal, even thickening from years of training
A thin shelf of tissue below the valve that leads out of the heart, causing a fixed blockage
A narrowed valve where blood leaves the heart (aortic stenosis)
differential.reveal: It is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction. One wall of his heart is 21 mm thick while the other is normal, and a valve flap is pulled into the path of the blood with each beat. Training thickens the heart evenly, and rarely past 13 to 15 mm. The murmur that gets louder when he bears down was the clue at the bedside: the heart fills less, and the blockage tightens.

terms.meaning: Overgrown. The muscle cells are larger than normal.
A disease of the heart muscle itself.
A blockage. Here the thick wall and a valve flap narrow the way out of the heart.

ending.stable: Home with his family, off the court for now, with an urgent heart center visit booked
ending.unstable: Seen by the heart specialists the same day, after a scare on the treadmill
ending.worse: Kept in hospital for heart monitoring
ending.critical: In the resuscitation room

cd-055.plainDiagnosis: An inherited thickening of the heart muscle that blocks blood leaving the heart (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with obstruction).

science.title: Why a thick wall becomes a blockage
science.text: Blood leaving his heart has to pass between the thick wall and the mitral valve. In a narrow channel the same flow has to move faster, and the pressure at its edges drops. That drop pulls the valve flap toward the wall, and the channel narrows further.

science.title: Why bearing down made the murmur louder
science.text: Bearing down squeezes the chest, and less blood returns to the heart. A less full heart is smaller, so the wall and the valve flap sit closer together and the blockage tightens. Squatting does the opposite: it pushes blood back to the heart, and his murmur softened.

science.title: Why his whole family needs a heart check
science.text: This condition is usually passed on by a single changed copy of a gene, so each child of an affected parent has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it. His father’s thick heart walls and his uncle’s sudden death fit that pattern. His own gene test has not been done yet.

sources.title: 2024 AHA/ACC guideline: management of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Frenneaux et al. (Circulation 1990): abnormal blood pressure response during exercise in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Conway et al. (Circulation 2023): exercise test abnormalities and outcomes in childhood hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: evaluation and management of patients with syncope

cd-061.title: Ten days of fever, _and now his breathing._

start.alarm: High fever · fast heart rate · low oxygen

cd-061.handoff: A 26-year-old man has had fevers and drenching sweats for ten days. For the last three days he has been short of breath, with chest pain when he breathes in. He injects heroin several times a day.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fevers and how he has been overall
interview.finding: Ten days of fever, drenching night sweats and exhaustion. He has no appetite and has lost about 4 kg without trying.

interview.prompt: Ask how he injects and what he may have been exposed to
interview.finding: He injects heroin several times a day and reuses needles. He has no stable place to live. He has never been tested for HIV.

interview.prompt: Ask about his chest and his breathing
interview.finding: For three days it has hurt to take a deep breath, and he has been getting more breathless. He coughs up phlegm that is sometimes streaked with blood.

exam.prompt: Listen to his heart and look at his neck veins
exam.finding: A soft whooshing sound (a murmur) runs through each beat, low on the left side of his breastbone. It gets louder when he breathes in. The veins in his neck are a little swollen.

exam.prompt: Listen to his lungs and watch his breathing
exam.finding: He is working a little harder than normal to breathe. There are crackling sounds scattered through both lungs.

exam.prompt: Look at his injection sites, and at his hands, feet and eyes
exam.finding: There are fresh and healed needle marks inside both elbows, with no skin infection around them. His nails, fingers, toes and the lining of his eyes show none of the small spots that a heart valve infection can cause.

1.label: Blood tests and chest X-ray
1.content:
White blood cells: 18.6, well above normal. That is a sign the body is fighting an infection.
Red blood cell level (hemoglobin): 10.4, mildly low.
Platelets and kidney function: normal.
Lactate: 2.4, slightly raised. It rises when the body is under strain from an infection.
Blood cultures (3 sets): still growing. No result yet.
Chest X-ray: many round patches near the edges of both lungs. Several have a hollow center.
Heart tracing (ECG): a fast but normal rhythm, with normal timing between the upper and lower chambers.
HIV test: not back yet.

0.resident: He looks sick. He has a fever of 39.1, a murmur and low oxygen. We need antibiotics in him soon, and one thing has to happen first.
0.question: What do we do before the first dose?
options: Start vancomycin now, and take blood cultures once his fever has gone
Draw at least three sets of blood cultures, each from a different vein
Send one blood culture and a urine culture
Start antibiotic tablets and book a heart ultrasound as an outpatient
0.fix: Draw three sets of blood cultures

terms.meaning: A sample of blood kept warm in a bottle of broth, to see whether bacteria grow. One “set” is two bottles filled from one needle stick.
Antibiotics chosen as a best guess, before the lab has named the bacteria.
A strong antibiotic given through a vein. It covers staph, including the resistant kind called MRSA.

outcomes.story: You ask the nurse to hang the vancomycin. The nurse is holding the culture bottles, and checks with the resident first.
outcomes.reply: Once an antibiotic is in his blood, the cultures may grow nothing, and we would be treating blind for weeks. Drawing them takes minutes. Cultures first, then the antibiotic straight after.

outcomes.story: Three sets are drawn from three separate veins, a few minutes apart. While that is done, the nurse starts oxygen through a small tube at his nose, and a chest X-ray and basic blood tests are sent. His oxygen level comes up.
outcomes.reply: Good. Three sets from separate sites give the lab the best chance of naming the bacteria. They also show whether it is in his blood all the time, which is the mark of an infection inside the heart or a blood vessel. The antibiotic follows as soon as the bottles are filled.

outcomes.story: You send one blood culture and a urine sample. The resident sees the single set on the trolley.
outcomes.reply: One set is not enough. If it grows a skin germ, we cannot tell contamination from real infection, and if it grows nothing we have learned little. Nothing points to his urine, either. Three sets, from three veins.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for antibiotic tablets and start his discharge papers. Half an hour later he is still waiting on the ward, breathing room air. His oxygen has dropped, and he cannot finish a sentence without stopping for breath.
outcomes.reply: He cannot go home. A fever, a murmur, low oxygen and failing breath mean an infection that is treated in hospital, with antibiotics through a vein and close watching. Oxygen on, cultures now, then the first dose.

3.resident: The picture is a heart valve infection that is sending infected clots to his lungs. The cultures are drawn. In someone who injects drugs, staph is the most likely germ, and it may be the resistant kind.
3.question: Which antibiotic has to be in the first treatment?
options: Vancomycin through a vein, to cover resistant staph (MRSA)
Ceftriaxone through a vein, on its own
Linezolid tablets
Ampicillin plus gentamicin through a vein

terms.meaning: A common skin bacterium. It is the usual cause of heart valve infection in people who inject drugs.
Staph that has become resistant to the penicillin family of antibiotics.
Switching from a broad antibiotic to the one that best fits the germ, once the lab has named it and tested it.

outcomes.story: The pharmacy sends the vancomycin up and the first dose is started. The infection specialists are called to help choose the rest of his treatment. He stays on oxygen and on the monitor.
outcomes.reply: Right. Until the lab says otherwise, we assume the staph may be resistant, and vancomycin covers that. When the cultures name the germ and show what kills it, the team will narrow to the antibiotic that fits best.

outcomes.story: You write the order for ceftriaxone alone. The pharmacist calls the ward.
outcomes.reply: Ceftriaxone does not kill resistant staph, and that is a real possibility for him. If we guess wrong, he gets days of the wrong drug while the infection damages his valve. The first treatment has to cover MRSA.

outcomes.story: You ask for linezolid tablets. The pharmacist calls before sending them.
outcomes.reply: Linezolid only holds staph back. It does not kill it outright. An infection on a heart valve is started on a drug that kills, given through a vein. He is also too sick to rely on tablets.

outcomes.story: You write the order for ampicillin with gentamicin. The pharmacist calls the ward.
outcomes.reply: That pair is aimed at other valve germs, such as enterococci. It misses resistant staph, and gentamicin can harm the kidneys. For him, staph cover comes first.

4.resident: The vancomycin is running. Now we need to look at the valve itself.
4.question: Which scan of his heart do we ask for first?
options: An ultrasound from inside the food pipe (TEE), skipping the one through the chest wall
An ultrasound through the chest wall (TTE)
An MRI of his heart
A CT scan of his chest in a week, to follow the patches in his lungs
4.fix: Ask for the ultrasound through the chest wall

terms.meaning: A clump of bacteria and clot stuck to a heart valve. Pieces can break off and travel in the blood.
Transthoracic echocardiogram: an ultrasound probe on the chest. It is quick and painless, and needs no sedation.
Transesophageal echocardiogram: a probe passed down the food pipe under sedation. It gives sharper pictures, and is used when the first scan is not enough.
The valve on the right side of the heart, between its upper and lower chambers. Blood from the veins passes through it on the way to the lungs.

outcomes.story: You request the scan through the food pipe. The heart ultrasound team calls back.
outcomes.reply: That scan needs sedation and a probe down the throat of a man who is short of breath. The scan through the chest wall is quick and safe, and it often shows the tricuspid valve well. We go on to the other one if the first is unclear, or if we still suspect more.

outcomes.story: The ultrasound team brings the machine to his bedside. He lies on his left side while they scan. The heart specialists will read it and decide whether a closer look from the food pipe is needed.
outcomes.reply: Good. We ask for it early. We do not wait for the lab to finish naming the germ. And a clear scan through the chest wall would not rule the infection out.

outcomes.story: You request a heart MRI. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: An MRI is slow, and he would have to lie flat in a tunnel while breathless. It is also not the test for finding clumps on a valve. Ultrasound is.

outcomes.story: You plan a chest CT for next week. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: The patches in his lungs came from somewhere. A lung scan next week tells us nothing about the valve they are breaking off from, and a week is a long time for a valve infection. We look at the heart now.

differential.resident: His blood tests and chest X-ray are in the chart. Put them together with the murmur and with how he got sick.
differential.question: What ties all of this together?
options: Pneumonia with fluid around the lung
Tuberculosis that has become active again
An infection on a right-sided heart valve, sending infected clots to the lungs
A blood clot in the lungs that has killed a patch of lung
differential.reveal: It is an infection on a heart valve on the right side of the heart. The murmur gets louder when he breathes in, which points to the tricuspid valve. Clumps break off that valve and are carried straight to the lungs, where they form the round, hollow patches on his X-ray. Pneumonia would not explain the murmur, or patches scattered through both lungs.

terms.meaning: An infection of the heart’s inner lining, usually on a valve.
Infected clumps that break off and lodge in blood vessels further on.
The side that receives blood from the veins and pumps it to the lungs. Whatever breaks off there goes to the lungs.

ending.stable: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics through a vein
ending.unstable: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics through a vein, being watched closely
ending.worse: On the ward, on oxygen and antibiotics, after getting worse while he waited
ending.critical: In intensive care

cd-061.plainDiagnosis: A staph infection on a heart valve on the right side of the heart (infective endocarditis), with infected clots carried to the lungs.

science.title: Why the infection landed in his lungs
science.text: Blood from his veins enters the right side of the heart, passes through the tricuspid valve and is pumped straight to the lungs. Bacteria injected into a vein reach that valve first, and anything that breaks off it is caught in the fine vessels of the lungs.

science.title: Why his oxygen was 91%
science.text: Each infected clump blocks and inflames a patch of lung. Oxygen crosses from air to blood only where the two meet across a thin, healthy wall, and he has fewer such places working. Less oxygen reaches his blood with every breath.

science.title: Why the team assumed resistant staph
science.text: Staph can carry a gene that makes the whole penicillin family useless against it, and bacteria can pass such genes to one another. Resistant staph is common enough that his first antibiotic had to cover it until the lab had tested his own.

sources.title: AHA scientific statement (2015): infective endocarditis in adults
AHA scientific statement (2022): management of infective endocarditis in people who inject drugs
2023 ESC guidelines: management of endocarditis

cd-019.title: Crushing chest pain, _three weeks after giving birth._

start.alarm: Severe chest pain · sweating

cd-019.handoff: A 39-year-old woman had her first baby three weeks ago. An hour ago, while she was resting, a crushing pain started in her chest and spread to her left arm. She is sweating and feels sick.

interview.prompt: Ask her to describe the chest pain
interview.finding: A heavy, crushing pressure behind her breastbone that spreads to her left arm. It started suddenly an hour ago while she was resting, with sweating and nausea, and it has not let up.

interview.prompt: Ask about the birth and the weeks since
interview.finding: Her first baby was born three weeks ago. The delivery was straightforward, and she is breastfeeding.

interview.prompt: Ask about her risks for heart and artery disease
interview.finding: She has no diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol. She has never smoked and does not use cocaine. No one in her family had early heart disease. An old kidney scan noted a mild irregularity in her artery walls (fibromuscular features).

exam.prompt: Check how she looks, and whether enough blood is reaching her body
exam.finding: She is frightened, sweating and still in pain. Her blood pressure is holding, and her hands and feet are warm.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and lungs
exam.finding: Her heartbeat is regular, with normal sounds and nothing extra. Her lungs are clear. There is no sign of fluid backing up.

exam.prompt: Feel the pulses on both sides and check her legs for a clot
exam.finding: Her pulses are equal on both sides. There is no whooshing sound over her arteries. Her legs are not swollen and her calves are not tender.

1.label: Heart tracing, blood tests and bedside scan
1.content:
Heart tracing (ECG): the pattern of a heart attack in progress (ST elevation) in the leads that look at the underside of the heart.
Blood test for heart damage (troponin): raised, and rising.
Red blood cell level and kidney function: normal.
Pregnancy test: negative.
Bedside heart ultrasound: the underside of the heart is not squeezing as it should. The overall squeeze is at the low end of normal (50%). There is no fluid around the heart.
She is taken straight to the catheter lab for dye pictures of her heart arteries (an angiogram).

0.resident: She is young and fit, with none of the usual risks. She also has crushing chest pain and she is drenched in sweat.
0.question: What happens in the next ten minutes?
options: Tell her a heart attack is unlikely at her age, and send her home
Send her for a CT scan first, to rule out a clot in her lungs
Give a clot-busting drug right away, before any tests
Get a heart tracing (ECG) and a blood test for heart damage now, and give aspirin
0.fix: Get the tracing, the blood test and aspirin

terms.meaning: Heart muscle dying because its blood supply has been cut off.
A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. It takes a few minutes and cannot hurt the patient.
A protein that leaks into the blood when heart muscle is damaged. It is the blood test for a heart attack.
A medicine that dissolves blood clots. It also raises the risk of bleeding anywhere in the body.

outcomes.story: You start to tell her it is probably not her heart. The resident is already wheeling in the tracing machine.
outcomes.reply: Young women have heart attacks too, and the weeks after childbirth carry risks of their own. Crushing pain with sweating gets a heart tracing within ten minutes, at any age.

outcomes.story: She is taken to the scanner. Her lungs are clear of clots. Forty minutes later she is back, gray and sweating, with the pain worse than before. No one has yet looked at her heart.
outcomes.reply: A lung clot was worth a thought so soon after a birth. But her pain is a classic heart pain, and the tracing takes two minutes. Her heart has gone forty more minutes without help. Tracing, blood test and aspirin, now.
outcomes.alarm: Pain getting worse · no heart tracing yet

outcomes.story: You ask for a clot-busting drug. The pharmacist will not release it without a heart tracing.
outcomes.reply: We never give that drug blind. We do not know yet that this is a heart attack, or what kind. In some heart attacks the problem is a tear in the artery wall, and a clot-buster can make a tear bleed and spread.

outcomes.story: The tracing is run at the bedside within minutes, blood is drawn and she chews an aspirin. The tracing shows a heart attack in progress. The heart team is called, and she is taken to the catheter lab for dye pictures of her arteries.
outcomes.reply: That is the right first move for anyone with chest pain like this. The tracing gave the answer in minutes, and the artery pictures will show us why it is happening.

3.resident: The pictures show a tear in the wall of her right heart artery, with blood trapped inside the wall. Blood is still flowing down the artery, her blood pressure is steady and her pain is easing.
3.question: How do we treat the torn artery?
options: Put stents along the whole torn section
Emergency bypass surgery, as for every torn heart artery
Medicines and close monitoring, keeping a procedure in reserve in case the blood flow fails
A full dose of a clot-busting drug to clear the blockage

terms.meaning: A tear in an artery’s inner lining that lets blood track into the wall itself.
A tiny mesh tube placed inside a narrowed artery to hold it open.
An operation that sews a new vessel around a blocked heart artery.
The room where doctors pass thin tubes into the heart’s arteries to take dye pictures and, if needed, to open a blockage.

outcomes.story: You ask the heart specialist to stent the whole tear. The specialist declines.
outcomes.reply: A torn artery is fragile. Wires and stents can push the tear further along, and the results are worse than in ordinary heart attacks. Most of these tears heal on their own within weeks to months. While blood is flowing, we leave it alone and watch.

outcomes.story: You call to book emergency bypass surgery. The heart surgeon asks about her blood flow, then says no.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is kept for tears in the main artery, or for when blood flow fails and a stent cannot fix it. Hers is in one artery, with blood still flowing. Open-heart surgery would add risk and no benefit right now.

outcomes.story: She is moved to the cardiac unit on a monitor, with medicines to ease the load on her heart. For a while her pain settles. Two hours later it comes back, hard, and the monitor alarms. The heart attack pattern has returned on her tracing, and her blood pressure is falling.
outcomes.reply: Watching closely was the right plan for a tear with good flow, and this is exactly what the watching is for. The tear has spread, or the trapped blood is squeezing the artery shut. The plan has to change.
outcomes.alarm: Chest pain back · blood pressure low

outcomes.story: You ask for a full dose of a clot-busting drug. The pharmacist calls the catheter lab to check.
outcomes.reply: There is no clot to dissolve. The artery is narrowed by blood trapped inside its own wall. A clot-buster can make that bleed more and spread the tear, so it is avoided in this condition.

4.resident: Her pain is back, the heart attack pattern on her tracing is not going away, and her blood pressure is 86 over 52.
4.question: What do we do now?
options: Take her back for new artery pictures now, and open the artery with a stent or surgery
Keep to the watching plan and give more pain relief
Send her home on a beta-blocker, with a clinic visit
Give a full dose of a clot-busting drug right away
4.fix: Take her back to the catheter lab

terms.meaning: Blood pressure falling, or the heart being starved of blood. An unstable patient cannot wait.
Restoring blood flow through a blocked artery, with a stent or with bypass surgery.
Blood pressure too low to supply the body’s organs.

outcomes.story: The team is called back, and she is in the catheter lab within minutes. The new pictures show the artery now almost closed. The specialists restore the blood flow. Her pain eases, the tracing settles and her blood pressure comes back up.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Watching is the plan only while she is stable and blood is flowing. Falling pressure and a heart attack that will not settle change that at once.

outcomes.story: You give more pain relief and keep watching. Half an hour later she is cold, clammy and barely answering. Her blood pressure has fallen further.
outcomes.reply: Pain relief quiets the alarm. It does not fix the artery. Her heart is being starved of blood, and it is failing as a pump. She goes back to the catheter lab now.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure very low · cold and clammy

outcomes.story: You start her discharge papers. The nurse looks at the monitor, then at you, and calls the resident.
outcomes.reply: She is having a heart attack in front of us, with falling blood pressure. No one in that state leaves the cardiac unit, let alone the hospital. She needs her artery opened.

outcomes.story: You ask for a clot-busting drug. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: It is still the wrong drug for a torn artery, because it can spread the tear. What she needs is the artery opened, in the catheter lab or the operating room.

5.resident: Her artery is open, and she is recovering in the cardiac unit. Before she goes home, we plan what comes next.
5.question: What do we check for, and what do we tell her?
options: Get a calcium scan of her heart arteries right away, to confirm fatty plaque
Start a strong statin and two platelet medicines for life, the same as after any heart attack
Tell her it will not happen again, and that she needs no follow-up
Scan her other arteries for fibromuscular dysplasia, and explain that a tear can happen again and that another pregnancy carries extra risk
5.fix: Scan her other arteries and talk it through

terms.meaning: A condition in which the walls of medium-sized arteries grow unevenly, which leaves them prone to narrowing, bulging or tearing. It is common in people who have had a torn heart artery.
A cholesterol-lowering medicine. It protects arteries that are clogged with fatty plaque.
The same problem happening again.

outcomes.story: You request a calcium scan. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: A calcium scan looks for hardened fatty plaque. Her heart attack was caused by a tear, and the pictures we already have showed that. There is no plaque to confirm.

outcomes.story: You write the standard after-heart-attack prescriptions for life. The heart specialist goes through them with you.
outcomes.reply: The standard package was built for arteries clogged with plaque. Hers tore. A statin is not routine here unless she has another reason for one, and her platelet medicines are chosen for her own case, which includes the fact that she is breastfeeding.

outcomes.story: You start to tell her it was a one-off. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: That is not true, and it would leave her unprotected. A torn heart artery can happen again. She needs to know the warning signs, and to be followed by people who know this condition.

outcomes.story: You sit down with her. Scans of the arteries from her head to her hips are booked. She hears that a tear can happen again, that chest pain always means calling for help, and that another pregnancy would carry extra risk and should be talked through with specialists first. Heart rehab is arranged.
outcomes.reply: That is what she needs to hear, said plainly and kindly. Her old kidney scan already hinted at fibromuscular dysplasia. Finding it elsewhere would change how she is followed for life.

differential.resident: The artery pictures are back. Her right heart artery has a long, smooth narrowing. Beside it is a thin flap, and dye is sitting inside the wall of the artery. There is no lump of plaque.
differential.question: What caused her heart attack?
options: A tear in the artery wall (spontaneous coronary artery dissection, or SCAD)
A fatty plaque that broke open and clotted
A spasm that clamped the artery shut for a while
A clot that formed in the heart and travelled into the artery
differential.reveal: It is a spontaneous coronary artery dissection, or SCAD. The inner lining of the artery tore, and blood tracked into the wall and squeezed the channel from the outside. That gives a long, smooth narrowing with a flap, not a ragged lump of plaque. It is the most common cause of a heart attack around pregnancy, and it often strikes young women with none of the usual risks.

terms.meaning: Happening on its own, with no injury and no procedure to cause it.
One of the arteries that feed the heart muscle.
A fatty build-up in an artery wall. It is the usual cause of heart attacks in older people.

ending.better: In the cardiac unit with her artery reopened, and a plan for the years ahead
ending.stable: In the cardiac unit with her artery reopened, and a plan for the years ahead
ending.unstable: In the cardiac unit, still being watched closely
ending.worse: In the cardiac unit, after a long wait for her heart attack to be found
ending.critical: In intensive care

cd-019.plainDiagnosis: A heart attack caused by a tear in the wall of a heart artery (spontaneous coronary artery dissection, or SCAD).

science.title: How a tear starves the heart without a clot
science.text: Blood that leaks into the artery’s wall is trapped there and bulges inward. The channel left for flowing blood gets narrower, and flow through a tube falls steeply as it narrows. The muscle fed by that artery runs short.

science.title: Why starved heart muscle fails so fast
science.text: Heart muscle makes almost all its ATP with oxygen. When her artery narrowed, the underside of her heart ran short within minutes and stopped squeezing properly. Cells that stay starved die and spill their troponin into the blood, which is what her blood test picked up.

science.title: Why her blood pressure fell when the artery closed
science.text: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps each minute. When more of her heart muscle lost its supply, each beat pushed out less. Her pressure dropped even as her heart beat faster to make up for it.

sources.title: AHA scientific statement (2018): spontaneous coronary artery dissection
Hayes et al. (JACC 2020): spontaneous coronary artery dissection, state-of-the-art review
ESC-ACCA position paper (2018): spontaneous coronary artery dissection
2025 ACC/AHA guideline: management of patients with acute coronary syndromes
2021 AHA/ACC guideline: evaluation and diagnosis of chest pain

cd-101.title: Dizzy every time _he stands up._
cd-101.handoff: A 73-year-old man has felt light-headed soon after getting up for the past three days. Yesterday he briefly collapsed, and came round as soon as he was lying down. He recently started a new blood pressure tablet.

interview.prompt: Ask what he is doing when it happens, and how he recovers
interview.finding: It comes on soon after he gets up, and eases when he lies down. After yesterday’s brief collapse he came round quickly once he was lying flat.

interview.prompt: Go through his medicines, how much he is drinking, and any bleeding
interview.finding: He recently started a thiazide, a water tablet for blood pressure. He has been drinking less during the hot weather. He has seen no bleeding. Either change could be playing a part. Neither is proven.

interview.prompt: Ask about warning signs of a heart cause
interview.finding: He has never collapsed during exercise. He has no chest pain and no racing or skipping heartbeat. No one in his family died suddenly at a young age.

exam.prompt: Check that it is safe to measure him standing
exam.finding: He is steady and comfortable lying down. He can stand with a member of staff beside him, who will help him back down if the dizziness comes on.

exam.prompt: Check how well filled he is, and listen to his heart and lungs
exam.finding: His mouth is a little dry. His pulse is regular, there is no significant murmur, and his lungs are clear.

exam.prompt: Look for injuries and check his nervous system
exam.finding: He has no injury from the collapse. His strength, sensation and speech are normal.

1.label: Lying and standing blood pressure, and heart tracing
1.content:
Lying down: 148/82.
After one minute standing: 112/64, with his usual light-headedness. That is a fall of 36 in the top number and 18 in the bottom one.
After three minutes standing: 118/68.
He was helped back to a safe position.
Heart tracing (ECG): a normal rhythm, with no problem reported in the timing or shape of the signals.
No sign of active bleeding, and no sudden chemical upset in his blood, was found.

4.label: Follow-up visit
4.content:
The team reviewed his tablets, dealt with his fluid intake in a way that suits his health, and gave advice on avoiding falls.
At his follow-up visit he is still getting light-headed on standing, despite those steps.
He has not been injured, and no new warning sign has appeared.

0.resident: His story points to his blood pressure dropping when he stands. Along with the questions about his collapse and a heart tracing, one measurement tests that idea directly.
0.question: Which measurement is it?
options: His sitting blood pressure at several visits, set beside his readings at home
His blood pressure in both arms while lying down, using the higher one
His blood pressure lying down, then again after at least a minute standing, noting any symptoms
His heart rate and oxygen level while he stands with support

terms.meaning: A drop in blood pressure on standing up. It is also called orthostatic hypotension.
Blood pressure is written as two numbers. The top one (systolic) is the pressure as the heart beats. The bottom one (diastolic) is the pressure between beats.
What the patient feels. A drop that brings on his usual light-headedness means more than a number alone.

outcomes.story: You start a chart for sitting readings over the next few visits. The resident looks at it.
outcomes.reply: Sitting readings tell us about his blood pressure in general. His trouble comes with the change from lying to standing, and a sitting cuff never sees that. We need a reading on each side of the change.

outcomes.story: You reach for a second cuff to check both arms. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Checking both arms answers other questions. Both readings would be taken lying down, so neither can show what happens when he stands.

outcomes.story: He rests lying down and you take his pressure. Then he stands, with a nurse at his elbow, and you measure again at one minute and at three. At one minute he says the light-headed feeling is back. He is helped down, and a heart tracing is done.
outcomes.reply: That is the test. Measure across the change in posture, keep him safe while you do it, and write down what he feels. A high reading lying down does not rule out a drop on standing.

outcomes.story: You clip on the oxygen probe and get ready to stand him up. The resident asks where the blood pressure cuff is.
outcomes.reply: Heart rate and oxygen are worth knowing, but they do not measure the thing we suspect. The idea is that his pressure falls. So we measure his pressure, lying and then standing.

3.resident: His pressure fell from 148 over 82 to 112 over 64 at one minute, and his symptoms came with it. His new water tablet and his low fluid intake are possible reasons, not proven ones.
3.question: What is the plan?
options: Adjust his treatment to bring down his lying blood pressure, and go over his sitting readings from home
Send him for nerve function tests before changing any medicine
Have him check his pressure at home for four weeks before looking into the dizziness
Review his tablets and his fluids, lower his risk of falling, and recheck his standing pressure
3.fix: Review tablets and fluids, and recheck him standing

terms.meaning: A water tablet for high blood pressure. It makes the kidneys pass more salt and water.
The nerves that adjust heart rate and blood vessels automatically, for example when a person stands up.
The chance of a fall and an injury. Dizziness on standing raises it, most of all in older people.

outcomes.story: You write up a stronger blood pressure plan aimed at his lying reading. The resident reads it before he leaves.
outcomes.reply: His lying reading is high, but his symptoms come from the fall on standing. Pushing his pressure lower would deepen that fall. When someone is dizzy on standing, we treat to the standing pressure.

outcomes.story: You request nerve function tests and leave his tablets as they are. The resident sets the request aside.
outcomes.reply: Those tests may be needed one day. But two likely and fixable reasons are in front of us: a new water tablet and too little fluid. We deal with those first and see what changes.

outcomes.story: You hand him a home blood pressure diary for the next four weeks. The resident stops him at the door.
outcomes.reply: He collapsed yesterday. Four weeks of waiting is four weeks in which he could fall and be badly hurt. We act on the likely causes today.

outcomes.story: The team goes through his tablets with him and adjusts them, and agrees how much he should drink given his health. You talk about getting up in stages, and what to do if the dizziness starts. A visit is booked to measure his standing pressure again.
outcomes.reply: Good. We treat what we found and what is likely behind it, without claiming we have proved the cause. The recheck on standing tells us whether it worked.

5.resident: He is back for his follow-up. He made the changes, and he is still getting light-headed when he stands. He has not fallen or hurt himself.
5.question: What do we do now?
options: Carry on with the same plan, and see him at next year’s blood pressure check
Look again for causes, and consider sending him to a specialist
Put the remaining spells down to simple faints, and book a tilt-table test
Treat it as failure of the autonomic nerves, and start treatment for that
5.fix: Look again and consider a specialist

terms.meaning: Go back over the story, the examination and the tests with fresh eyes when a plan has not worked.
The measured drop in pressure is a finding. Why it happens is the cause. Knowing the first does not settle the second.
A test that tilts a patient upright, while they are watched, to bring on a faint. It is for cases where the cause is unclear.

outcomes.story: You book him in for next year. The resident looks at the date.
outcomes.reply: The plan has not worked, and he is at risk of a fall every day. Symptoms that persist after the obvious causes are dealt with need a fresh look now, not in a year.

outcomes.story: You go back over his story, his medicines and his examination, and repeat his lying and standing pressures. The resident agrees that he should also be seen by a specialist, and you explain to him why.
outcomes.reply: Right. The first measurement was useful, and it still stands. But a finding is not a full explanation, and when the simple fixes fail we widen the search.

outcomes.story: You write “simple faints” in his notes and request a tilt-table test. The resident reads the note.
outcomes.reply: Nothing new points to simple faints. His spells still come with standing, as before. Changing the label without new evidence would send the search down the wrong road.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for an autonomic failure medicine. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: That is a diagnosis nobody has made. His drop in pressure has several possible causes, and nerve failure is only one of them. We find out first, and treat after.

differential.resident: His lying and standing readings and his heart tracing are in the chart. Work out the size of the drop, then tell me what fits.
differential.question: What is the best working diagnosis?
options: A drop in blood pressure on standing (postural hypotension), with causes that may be fixable
Failure of the nerves that control blood pressure (primary autonomic failure)
A dangerous heart rhythm that comes and goes
Simple faints brought on by standing a long time in the heat
differential.reveal: It fits a drop in blood pressure on standing. The top number fell by 36 and the bottom by 18 within a minute, and his usual symptoms came with it. A fall of 20 or more in the top number counts. This tells us what is happening. It does not yet tell us why, and it does not rule out every other cause.

terms.meaning: The best explanation for now. It is changed if new facts do not fit.
Low blood pressure.

ending.stable: Referred to a specialist, with a plan to keep him safe from falls
ending.worse: Kept in for more checks
ending.critical: In the resuscitation room

cd-101.plainDiagnosis: A drop in blood pressure on standing (postural hypotension) that makes him light-headed. Its cause is still being worked out.

science.title: Why standing up tests the circulation
science.text: When he stands, the veins in his legs sit under a tall column of blood, and the pressure inside them rises. They stretch and hold more blood, so less returns to the heart and it has less to pump up to the brain. A healthy body corrects this within seconds. His did not.

science.title: How a water tablet and hot weather could add up
science.text: A thiazide makes his kidneys pass more salt, and water follows the salt. He was also drinking less in the heat. Both would leave less fluid in his circulation, and so less blood to refill the heart when he stands. This is a likely explanation. It has not been proven.

science.title: What should have happened when he stood
science.text: Sensors in the large arteries detect a fall in pressure and signal the heart to speed up and the blood vessels to tighten. That reflex normally holds the pressure steady. In him it still fell by 36, so either the reflex had too little blood to work with or it is not working fully. The follow-up is there to find out which.

sources.title: NICE NG136: hypertension in adults, measuring blood pressure and postural hypotension (recommendations amended 2023)
NICE CG109: transient loss of consciousness, initial assessment
Consensus statement (Clin Auton Res 2011): definition of orthostatic hypotension
2017 ACC/AHA/HRS guideline: evaluation and management of patients with syncope

nr-011.title: The room spins _when she rolls over._
nr-011.handoff: A 58-year-old woman has had a week of brief spinning spells. Each one starts when she rolls over in bed or looks up, lasts about half a minute and then stops completely.

interview.prompt: Ask what sets the spinning off and how long it lasts
interview.finding: It starts a few seconds after she rolls onto her right side, looks up to a high shelf or bends to tie her shoes. The room whirls for 20 to 40 seconds, then stops completely.

interview.prompt: Ask about her hearing and her ears
interview.finding: No hearing loss, no ringing and no feeling of fullness in either ear.

interview.prompt: Ask about signs of a brain problem
interview.finding: No headache, double vision or slurred speech. No numbness, no weakness and no trouble walking between spells.

exam.prompt: Watch her eyes for jerking movements while she sits still
exam.finding: Her eyes are steady, whether she looks straight ahead or to the side. Nothing abnormal shows while she sits quietly between spells.

exam.prompt: Test her walking and her coordination
exam.finding: She touches her nose and your finger accurately, walks steadily, can walk heel to toe, and stands steady with her feet together and her eyes closed.

exam.prompt: Check her hearing and look in her ears
exam.finding: She hears a finger rub equally on both sides. Both eardrums look normal.

1.label: Positioning test
1.content:
Head turned to the right and lowered back quickly (the Dix-Hallpike test, right ear down): after a 5-second pause, her eyes beat upward and twist toward the right ear for about 20 seconds, and her spinning comes on. Repeating it straight away gives a weaker response.
The same test with the left ear down: no eye movements and no spinning.
Rolling her head from side to side while she lies flat: no sideways eye movements.

0.resident: Her spells are short, they come with a change in head position, and she is completely well in between. Her exam just now was normal.
0.question: How do we test this?
options: An MRI of her brain and inner ears
Lay her back quickly with her head turned, and watch her eyes (the Dix-Hallpike test)
A full hearing test
An ultrasound of the arteries in her neck

terms.meaning: A false feeling that you or the room are spinning.
The patient is laid back quickly with the head turned to one side and hanging slightly below the table. If loose crystals are in that ear’s canal, the eyes jerk in a telltale pattern.
Rhythmic jerking of the eyes. Its direction and timing show which part of the balance system is misfiring.

outcomes.story: You fill in the request for an MRI. The resident reads it before it is sent.
outcomes.reply: A scan is for vertigo that does not stop, or that comes with hearing loss in one ear or signs of a brain problem. She has none of those. A bedside test can answer this in a minute.

outcomes.story: You explain that the test may bring the spinning on for a few seconds. With her head turned to the right, you lay her back quickly and watch her eyes. Then you repeat it to the left. What you saw goes in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Good. It takes seconds and needs no machine. It shows whether this is the crystal problem, and which ear it is in.

outcomes.story: You book a full hearing test. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: A hearing test is for dizziness that comes with hearing loss, ringing or ear fullness. She has none of those. It would not explain her spells.

outcomes.story: You request a scan of her neck arteries. The resident sets the form aside.
outcomes.reply: Those arteries feed the front of the brain. Dizziness from poor blood flow comes from the arteries at the back, and it does not switch on and off with rolling over. This test would tell us nothing.

3.resident: The test brought on her spinning with the right ear down, and her eyes did exactly what loose crystals make them do.
3.question: How do we treat it?
options: Guide her head through a set of positions to roll the crystals out (the Epley maneuver)
Meclizine three times a day for two weeks
A course of steroid tablets
A low-salt diet and a water tablet

terms.meaning: Tiny grains of calcium carbonate that normally sit on a sensor in the inner ear and help it detect gravity.
Three fluid-filled loops in each inner ear that sense head turns.
A medicine that dulls the balance system. It can ease nausea, but it does not move the crystals.

outcomes.story: You check that her neck and back can manage the movements. Then you guide her head through four positions, holding each for about half a minute. She is dizzy at first, and it fades by the last position. You give her advice on avoiding falls, and book a visit in a few weeks to see how she is.
outcomes.reply: That treats the cause. The movements roll the loose crystals out of the canal, to a place where they no longer set off the sensor. It often works in one or two sessions.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for meclizine. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: Meclizine dulls the whole balance system. It does not move the crystals, and it can leave her drowsy and unsteady. Guidelines advise against using it routinely for this.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for steroids. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: Steroids are sometimes used for an inflamed balance nerve, which causes spinning that lasts for days. Hers lasts seconds and comes from loose crystals. Steroids do nothing for that.

outcomes.story: You start writing advice on a low-salt diet and a water tablet. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment for Ménière’s disease, where the spinning lasts for hours and comes with hearing loss and ringing. She has none of that.

4.resident: Three months have passed. The maneuver cleared her spinning, and now the same brief spells are back when she rolls to the right. The positioning test shows the same pattern as before.
4.question: What do we do this time?
options: An MRI of her brain and inner ears
Send her for surgery to plug the canal
Start meclizine every day, to be taken indefinitely
Repeat the Epley maneuver

terms.meaning: The same problem coming back after it had cleared.
An operation that blocks the affected canal. It is kept for rare cases that keep coming back despite many maneuvers.

outcomes.story: You request an MRI. The resident reads the request.
outcomes.reply: These are the same spells with the same test result, and nothing new. That is the crystal problem again, and a scan would add nothing. New or different symptoms would change that.

outcomes.story: You start a referral to the ear surgeons. The resident stops it.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is a last resort for rare cases that do not respond. One return after three good months is common, and the maneuver worked well for her last time.

outcomes.story: You write a long-term prescription for meclizine. The pharmacist calls the clinic.
outcomes.reply: Taking it every day would leave her drowsy, and would slow her balance system’s own recovery. It still would not move the crystals.

outcomes.story: You repeat the maneuver, and her spinning settles again. You show her what to watch for, go over the advice on falls once more, and book a check in a month.
outcomes.reply: Right. This often comes back, and the answer is the same maneuver. We still check each time that it really is the same problem and not something new.

differential.resident: The positioning test is in her chart. Look at what her eyes did, and on which side.
differential.question: What is causing her spinning?
options: An inflamed balance nerve (vestibular neuritis): constant spinning for days
Ménière’s disease: attacks lasting hours, with hearing loss and ringing
Loose crystals in the right inner ear (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV)
Vestibular migraine: dizzy spells in someone who gets migraines
A drop in blood pressure on standing
differential.reveal: It is BPPV, in her right ear. Tiny crystals have come loose and drifted into one of the balance canals. When she moves her head a certain way they roll, and the canal reports a spin that is not happening. The short delay, the eye movements toward the lower ear and the fading on repeat testing are its signature.

terms.meaning: Not dangerous.
Coming in sudden, short bursts.
Brought on by a change in the position of the head.

ending.stable: Going home steady, with a check booked in a month
ending.worse: Kept for more tests
ending.critical: In the emergency department

nr-011.plainDiagnosis: Brief spinning spells caused by loose crystals in the right inner ear (benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, or BPPV).

science.title: Why a head turn became a spin
science.text: Each balance canal holds fluid and a sensor that bends when the fluid moves. Her loose crystals roll when she tips her head, and they drag the fluid along. The sensor bends and reports a turn that her eyes and body do not confirm, and that mismatch is felt as spinning.

science.title: Why the maneuver works
science.text: The crystals are denser than the fluid around them, so they sink. Each position in the maneuver tilts the canal so that gravity carries them further along it, until they drop out of the canal altogether.

sources.title: AAO-HNS clinical practice guideline (2017 update): benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
GRACE-3 guideline (2023): acute dizziness and vertigo in the emergency department

nr-025.title: A first seizure, _in front of his coworkers._
nr-025.handoff: A 24-year-old man had a convulsion at work, in front of his coworkers. He was confused for about 20 minutes afterward. He is back to normal now and wants to go home.

interview.prompt: Ask his coworker exactly what happened
interview.finding: He cried out, went stiff and fell. All four limbs shook for 60 to 90 seconds, with froth at his mouth, and he wet himself. He was confused and groggy for about 20 minutes afterward.

interview.prompt: Ask about anything that could have set it off
interview.finding: He has been sleeping only three or four hours a night to finish a project. He uses no drugs. He has not been drinking heavily and has not just stopped. He has had no head injury, fever or headache.

interview.prompt: Ask about earlier seizures and his family
interview.finding: He has never had a seizure before and takes no medicines. No one in his family has epilepsy or died suddenly.

exam.prompt: Check how well he has recovered, and look for injuries
exam.finding: He is fully awake and himself again. There is a fresh bite on the left side of his tongue.

exam.prompt: Do a full check of his nervous system
exam.finding: His eye movements, face, speech, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination and walking are all normal.

exam.prompt: Look for signs of infection or other illness
exam.finding: His neck is not stiff, light does not bother him and he has no rash. His heart and lungs are normal.

1.label: Blood tests, scans and brain-wave test
1.content:
Blood sugar: 96, normal.
Blood salts (sodium, calcium, magnesium): normal.
Drug screen: negative. Blood alcohol: none found.
CT and MRI of his brain: normal, with no injury, bleeding or growth.
Brain-wave test (EEG): normal, with none of the spikes that can mark a tendency to seizures.

0.resident: He is awake, safe and breathing well. Now we have to find out why this happened.
0.question: What do we check?
options: Start an antiseizure medicine now, before any tests
Send him home now with no tests
Check his blood sugar and salts, look for triggers, and get a brain scan and a brain-wave test (EEG)
Do a spinal tap, as for every first seizure
0.fix: Check sugar and salts, then scan and EEG

terms.meaning: A burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It can cause stiffening, shaking and loss of awareness.
A seizure with an immediate cause, such as very low blood sugar, a salt imbalance, a drug or alcohol withdrawal.
A recording of the brain’s electrical activity, made through small sensors on the scalp.
A needle in the lower back to sample the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It looks for infection or bleeding.

outcomes.story: You write the order for an antiseizure medicine. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: Not yet. If this seizure had a fixable cause, like low blood sugar or a salt imbalance, he would not need the medicine at all. We find out why first.

outcomes.story: You start his discharge papers. The resident takes them.
outcomes.reply: He feels fine, but a first seizure can be the first sign of something treatable: a chemical imbalance, a drug, a growth, a bleed. We do not send him home without looking.

outcomes.story: A fingerstick sugar is done at once and blood is sent. You go back over possible triggers with him and his coworker. He has a CT and then an MRI, and the EEG team records his brain waves. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: That covers the causes we can fix, and it tells us about his risk of another seizure. An MRI is the better scan for this. A CT is the fast one.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: A spinal tap is for a suspected brain infection or bleed: fever, a stiff neck, a weak immune system, a sudden terrible headache. He has none of those. It is not a routine test after a first seizure.

3.resident: Every test is normal, and nothing we can find set this off. He asks whether he has to start medicine.
3.question: What do we tell him about medicine?
options: Talk through the benefits and risks with him. Holding off, with a prompt visit to a neurologist, is a reasonable choice
Yes: medicine for life is required after any seizure
Yes: start two medicines, to be sure of control
Yes: admit him for a levetiracetam drip

terms.meaning: A daily medicine that makes seizures less likely. It does not cure their cause.
The chance of another seizure. It is highest in the first two years.
A doctor who specializes in the brain and nerves.

outcomes.story: You sit down with him. Medicine now would lower his chance of another seizure over the next two years. It is unlikely to change his long-term outlook, and it can have side effects. He thinks about his job and decides to hold off for now. A neurology visit is booked.
outcomes.reply: That is the honest conversation. Either choice can be right, and it is his to make once he knows the facts. Normal tests do not mean no risk.

outcomes.story: You tell him he will need medicine for life. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: One seizure is not epilepsy, and many people never have another. Treatment after a first seizure is a choice made with the patient. It is not automatic, and it is not for life.

outcomes.story: You write for two antiseizure medicines. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: When treatment is started, it is with one medicine. Two at once add side effects, and no one has shown that he needs even one.

outcomes.story: You ask for a bed and a levetiracetam drip. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: A drip is for someone who is still seizing or cannot swallow. He has recovered fully. He does not need a hospital bed for a decision that is made in a conversation.

4.resident: He is ready to go home. What he does over the next few months matters more than anything we did today.
4.question: What is the most important thing to tell him?
options: He can drive right away, with no limits
Follow the local driving rules after a seizure, do not swim alone or work at unprotected heights, and get enough sleep
He must give up work for good
A moderate amount of alcohol will help prevent another seizure

terms.meaning: Avoiding places where a sudden blackout could kill: deep water alone, heights, dangerous machinery, a bath with a baby.
A set period without driving after a seizure. Its length is set by local law.
Something that makes a seizure more likely, such as lost sleep or heavy drinking.

outcomes.story: You tell him he is fine to drive home. The resident stops him at the door.
outcomes.reply: A second seizure at the wheel could kill him or someone else. The law sets a seizure-free period before driving again, and it varies from place to place. He needs to know that before he leaves.

outcomes.story: You go through it with him and his coworker: no driving until the law allows it, no swimming alone, no ladders or roofs, and regular sleep. He knows to come back if it happens again, and that a seizure lasting more than five minutes means calling an ambulance.
outcomes.reply: That is the advice that keeps him alive if there is a second seizure. Too little sleep may have played a part this time, so it is worth fixing.

outcomes.story: You tell him he will have to stop working. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: That goes far beyond the evidence. He is a graphic designer with one seizure and normal tests. He can work. He needs sensible precautions, not the loss of his job.

outcomes.story: You tell him a drink or two will help. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Alcohol does not prevent seizures. Heavy drinking, and the withdrawal after it, both make one more likely. The advice is to go easy on it.

differential.resident: All his results are in the chart. Put them together with what his coworkers saw.
differential.question: How do we classify what happened?
options: A provoked seizure: set off by an immediate cause such as low sugar, a drug or alcohol
Epilepsy: an established tendency to repeated seizures
A non-epileptic event: one that looks like a seizure without the abnormal electrical activity
A first unprovoked seizure: a real seizure with no immediate cause found
differential.reveal: It is a first unprovoked seizure. The cry, the stiffening and shaking, the bitten side of the tongue and the long confusion afterward all point to a real seizure, and no immediate cause was found. One seizure is not yet epilepsy. Normal scans and a normal EEG do not rule epilepsy out, either.

terms.meaning: With no immediate cause, such as low blood sugar, a drug or a fresh injury.
A lasting tendency to have unprovoked seizures. It is usually diagnosed after two, or after one when the risk of another is high.

ending.stable: Going home with safety advice and a neurology visit booked
ending.worse: Kept in for observation
ending.critical: In the resuscitation room

nr-025.plainDiagnosis: A first seizure with no immediate cause found (a first unprovoked seizure).

science.title: What a seizure is at the level of a cell
science.text: A nerve cell fires when ions rush through channels in its membrane. Normally the cells that excite their neighbors are held in check by cells that quiet them. In his seizure that balance failed for a minute and a half, and huge numbers of cells fired together.

science.title: Why his blood sugar was the first test
science.text: The brain runs almost entirely on glucose and keeps almost none in reserve. A very low blood sugar can starve nerve cells of fuel within minutes and set off a seizure. His was a normal 96, so that was not the cause.

science.title: Why he remembers none of it
science.text: Storing a memory needs orderly activity in the brain’s memory circuits. During the seizure and the confused spell after it, that activity was disrupted, so nothing was stored. A gap like his is typical after this kind of seizure.

sources.title: AAN/AES guideline (2015): management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults
AAN/AES practice parameter (2007): evaluating an apparent unprovoked first seizure in adults
ILAE official report (2014): a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

nr-012.title: Spinning _that will not stop._

start.alarm: Constant spinning · vomiting

nr-012.handoff: A 45-year-old man has had constant, severe spinning for 18 hours. He has vomited four times and cannot walk straight. He had a cold about a week ago.

interview.prompt: Ask how long it has lasted, and whether position changes it
interview.finding: It has been constant for 18 hours. It is there even when he lies perfectly still, and any head movement makes it much worse. He has vomited four times.

interview.prompt: Ask about his hearing and his ears
interview.finding: No change in hearing, no ringing and no feeling of fullness in either ear.

interview.prompt: Ask about signs of a stroke, and his risks for one
interview.finding: No headache, neck pain, double vision, slurred speech, trouble swallowing, numbness or weakness. He has high blood pressure and has smoked a pack a day for 20 years.

exam.prompt: Watch his eyes for jerking movements
exam.finding: When he looks straight ahead, his eyes drift and jerk sideways, beating to the left. The jerking gets stronger when he looks left and weaker when he looks right, and it settles when he fixes on a target.

exam.prompt: Test his face, speech, hearing, strength and coordination
exam.finding: His hearing, speech and face are normal. His arms and legs are strong, and he touches his nose and your finger accurately.

exam.prompt: Watch him stand and walk
exam.finding: He can stand without help. When he walks, he veers to the right.

1.label: Bedside eye tests
1.content:
Head impulse test (a quick, small turn of the head while he stares at the examiner’s nose): when his head is turned to the right, his eyes slip off target and have to jump back. Turned to the left, they stay on target.
Eye jerking: it always beats to the left, whichever way he looks. It gets stronger looking left and settles when he fixes on a target.
Cover test (covering each eye in turn): no vertical shift of either eye.
Hearing to a finger rub: normal on both sides.
Blood sugar: 108, normal.

0.resident: This is constant spinning with jerking eyes. It is usually an inner-ear nerve problem, but a stroke at the back of the brain can look just like it. A doctor trained in the bedside eye exam is here.
0.question: How do we tell the two apart?
options: A CT scan of his head
An MRI of his brain right away
The three-part bedside eye exam (HINTS)
Lay him back with his head turned (the Dix-Hallpike test)
A full hearing test

terms.meaning: Three bedside checks of the eyes: a quick head turn, the direction of the eye jerking, and a cover test. In trained hands they separate an inner-ear problem from a stroke.
The nerve that carries balance signals from the inner ear to the brain.

terms.term: Stroke at the back of the brain
terms.meaning: A blocked artery to the brainstem or cerebellum, the parts that handle balance and coordination.

outcomes.story: You request a CT of his head. The resident stops the request.
outcomes.reply: A CT misses most early strokes at the back of the brain, so a normal result would reassure us falsely. Guidelines advise against it for this.

outcomes.story: You request an urgent MRI. The resident holds the request.
outcomes.reply: An MRI is the right test if the bedside exam points to the brain or is unclear. But it can miss a small stroke in the first day or two, and a trained examiner at the bedside does at least as well. The exam comes first.

outcomes.story: The trained doctor does the three checks while you watch, and tests his hearing with a finger rub. Each step is explained to him first, because the head turn makes the spinning worse for a moment. The findings go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. In constant spinning with jerking eyes, these three checks are the best first test, as long as the examiner is trained. Any result that points to the brain, or is unclear, means an urgent MRI.

outcomes.story: You get ready to lay him back with his head turned. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: That test is for brief spells set off by position. His spinning is constant, so it would only make him vomit and would tell us nothing.

outcomes.story: You book a full hearing test. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: His hearing is normal to a simple finger rub, and a formal test will not separate an ear problem from a stroke. It can wait.

3.resident: The bedside exam points to the balance nerve on the right, and nothing points to the brain.
3.question: How do we treat him?
options: A clot-busting drug, as for a stroke
Meclizine around the clock for four weeks
Surgery to relieve pressure at the back of the brain
Anti-sickness and calming medicines for no more than three days, early movement with balance exercises, and a talk about a short steroid course

terms.meaning: A medicine such as meclizine that dulls the balance system and eases spinning and nausea.
Head and eye movements that train the brain to adjust to a weak balance nerve.
The brain’s gradual adjustment to a lopsided balance signal. It needs movement to happen.

outcomes.story: You ask for a clot-busting drug. The pharmacist calls the stroke team, who say no.
outcomes.reply: That drug is for a stroke, and it can cause bleeding in the brain. His exam points to the balance nerve. We do not give it without a stroke to treat.

outcomes.story: You write for meclizine around the clock for a month. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: A few days of relief is kind. A month is harmful. The brain learns to adjust to a weak balance nerve by moving, and a drug that dulls the system slows that down.

outcomes.story: You call the brain surgeons. The resident takes the phone.
outcomes.reply: That operation is for a large stroke at the back of the brain that is swelling. Nothing here points to one.

outcomes.story: He gets fluid through a vein and an anti-sickness medicine, and the vomiting stops. Once he can sit up, a therapist starts him on simple head and eye movements. You explain that a short steroid course is an option with uncertain benefit, and he chooses to try it. He knows which new symptoms should bring him straight back.
outcomes.reply: That is the balance: ease the worst of it for a day or two, then get him moving. And we keep an open mind. If anything new appears, such as double vision, slurred speech, weakness or hearing loss, the stroke question is open again.

4.resident: One more thing before he goes. I want you to know which finding would have sent him straight for an MRI and a full stroke workup.
4.question: Which one is it?
options: Spinning that had lasted more than 24 hours
Eyes that stayed on target during the quick head turn, on both sides
Eye jerking that settled when he fixed on a target
Vomiting more than three times
Veering to one side while still able to walk without help

terms.meaning: A quick, small turn of the head while the patient stares at a target. A healthy balance nerve keeps the eyes locked on. A weak one lets them slip, so they have to jump back.

terms.term: A normal test that is bad news
terms.meaning: In constant spinning, eyes that stay on target mean the balance nerve is working. The fault is then more likely to be in the brain.

outcomes.story: You say it is the 24-hour mark. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: How long it lasts does not separate the two. A balance nerve problem often spins for days. The warning sign is a quick head turn that looks normal on both sides, because then the nerve is working and the fault is likely in the brain.

outcomes.story: You say it is a normal head turn test on both sides. The resident nods.
outcomes.reply: Yes. It sounds backward, and it is the heart of this exam. In a patient who is spinning constantly, a normal test is the worrying result. Eye jerking that changes direction, a vertical shift on the cover test, or being unable to stand at all would worry us too.

outcomes.story: You say it is jerking that settles when he fixes on something. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a reassuring sign, typical of an inner-ear problem. The warning sign is a quick head turn that looks normal on both sides.

outcomes.story: You say it is the vomiting. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Vomiting tells us how miserable he is. It does not tell us where the problem is. The warning sign is a quick head turn that looks normal on both sides.

outcomes.story: You say it is the veering. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Veering toward the weak side while still walking fits a balance nerve problem. Being unable to stand at all would be a different matter. The warning sign is a quick head turn that looks normal on both sides.

differential.resident: The bedside tests are in his chart. Three things matter: what the quick head turn showed, which way his eyes beat, and the cover test.
differential.question: What is the most likely cause?
options: An inflamed balance nerve on the right (vestibular neuritis)
A stroke at the back of the brain on the right
An inflamed inner ear on the right (labyrinthitis): the same, but with hearing loss
Loose crystals in the inner ear (BPPV): brief spells set off by position
Ménière’s disease: attacks lasting hours, with hearing loss and ringing
differential.reveal: The best fit is an inflamed balance nerve on the right. His eyes slipped when his head was turned to the right, the jerking always beat the same way, the cover test was normal and his hearing is intact. That pattern points to the nerve and not the brain. It is the most likely answer, not a guarantee, so he is watched for anything new.

terms.meaning: Inflammation of the balance nerve, often after a viral illness. It causes days of constant spinning without hearing loss.
The same problem with the hearing part of the inner ear involved as well.

ending.better: Going home steadier, with balance exercises and clear warning signs to watch for
ending.stable: Going home steadier, with balance exercises and clear warning signs to watch for
ending.worse: Kept in for a brain scan
ending.critical: In the stroke unit

nr-012.plainDiagnosis: Constant spinning from an inflamed balance nerve on the right (vestibular neuritis).

science.title: Why losing one balance nerve feels like spinning
science.text: Each inner ear sends the brain a steady stream of signals, and the brain reads a difference between the two sides as a head turn. With his right nerve inflamed, the right side went quiet. The brain reads that lopsided signal as a constant turn to the left, even while he lies still.

science.title: Why steroids were offered as a maybe
science.text: In one trial, steroids helped the balance nerve recover more of its function on testing. Whether patients feel or function better in the long run has not been shown. A better test result and a better life are different claims, which is why this was his choice to make.
science.lessonTitle: Decide what a study can claim

sources.title: GRACE-3 guideline (2023): acute dizziness and vertigo in the emergency department
Kattah et al. (Stroke 2009): HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome
Strupp et al. (NEJM 2004): methylprednisolone, valacyclovir, or the combination for vestibular neuritis

nr-016.title: Knocked out, woke up, _now fading._

start.alarm: Getting drowsier · left pupil larger · slow heart rate

nr-016.handoff: A 22-year-old man was hit on the left side of the head with a bat 90 minutes ago. He was knocked out for a minute, then woke up and talked normally. Over the last half hour he has become confused and very sleepy.

interview.prompt: Ask the paramedics what happened right after the blow
interview.finding: He was hit over the left temple and was out for about a minute. Then he woke, stood up and talked normally. He even argued with bystanders before he started to get worse.

interview.prompt: Ask how he has changed since then
