interview.finding: Over the last 30 minutes he has had a severe, worsening headache on the left, has vomited twice, and has become confused and more and more sleepy.

interview.prompt: Ask about medicines and bleeding problems
interview.finding: He takes no medicines and no blood thinners, and has no known bleeding disorder. He had two beers earlier in the evening.

exam.prompt: Check how awake he is, and look at his pupils
exam.finding: He is drowsy and sometimes agitated. He opens his eyes to your voice, his words do not make sense, and he pushes your hand away when you press on his nail (a coma score of 11 out of 15). His left pupil is large and slow to react. The right is normal.

exam.prompt: Test the strength in his arms and legs
exam.finding: His right arm drifts down when he holds both out, and his right side is weaker than his left. His right big toe turns up when the sole is stroked, a sign of pressure on the brain’s movement pathway.

exam.prompt: Look at his head for signs of injury
exam.finding: There is a soft, swollen bruise over his left temple. There is no bruising behind his ears or around his eyes yet.

1.label: CT scan and clotting tests
1.content:
CT scan of the head: a lens-shaped collection of fresh blood between the skull and the brain’s outer covering, on the left side, 22 mm thick. It stops at the seams of the skull. The bone over it is cracked.
The blood has pushed the brain 9 mm off center, squeezed the fluid space on the left and begun to force the inner edge of the brain downward.
No bleeding inside the brain tissue itself.
Clotting tests and platelets: normal.

0.resident: His airway, breathing and circulation have been checked and are secure for now. He is getting worse in front of us, and his left pupil is larger than his right.
0.question: What is the very next step?
options: A spinal tap, to look for bleeding around the brain
An emergency CT scan of his head
An MRI of his brain
Give mannitol through a vein and watch him for an hour

terms.meaning: A stretch of normal wakefulness between a head injury and a later collapse. It is a warning sign of bleeding inside the skull.
A pupil that widens and stops reacting to light, because the nerve to it is being squeezed by a swollen or shifted brain.
A medicine that draws water out of the brain and lowers the pressure in the skull for a short time.
A needle in the lower back to sample the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It looks for infection or bleeding.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you before it is opened.
outcomes.reply: Never, with a pupil like that. Something is pressing on his brain from above. Draining fluid from below could pull the brain downward and kill him.

outcomes.story: He is taken straight to the scanner, with a nurse and the resident beside him. The scan takes minutes. The neurosurgeon is called while the pictures are still coming up.
outcomes.reply: Right. A CT is fast and shows fresh blood clearly. And we call the neurosurgeon now, without waiting for the report.

outcomes.story: He is slid into the MRI scanner, where no one can reach him easily. Halfway through he stops answering. He is pulled out barely rousable, with his left pupil wider than before.
outcomes.reply: An MRI takes far too long for a man who is getting worse by the minute, and he cannot be watched properly inside it. A CT shows this kind of bleeding in seconds. He goes there now.

outcomes.story: The mannitol goes in, and for a while he seems a little brighter. Before the hour is up he is harder to wake than before, and his right side is weaker.
outcomes.reply: Mannitol buys minutes. It does not stop an artery bleeding inside his skull. We have spent an hour and still do not know what we are treating. He needs the scan and a neurosurgeon now.
outcomes.alarm: Harder to wake · right side weaker

3.resident: The scan shows a large collection of blood pressing on his brain and pushing it 9 mm off center. His clotting is normal. The neurosurgeon is looking at the pictures.
3.question: What will actually fix this?
options: Emergency surgery to open the skull and remove the blood
Admit him for regular checks, and repeat the CT in six hours
A dose of antiseizure medicine and blood pressure control, and nothing else
Cool his body in intensive care (therapeutic hypothermia)

terms.meaning: An operation that opens a window in the skull so the surgeon can remove a clot and stop the bleeding.
How far the brain has been pushed off center. More than 5 mm is a sign that surgeons act on.
Part of the brain being forced out of its normal compartment by pressure. It crushes vital structures, and is quickly fatal if it is not relieved.

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon looks at the scan and books the operating room at once. While it is being readied he gets worse again: his left pupil is wider and his right side is weaker than when the scan was done.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is the only thing that fixes this, and the decision was made without delay. But the blood is still collecting, and he is getting worse faster than the room can be set up. We have to buy him those minutes.
outcomes.alarm: Getting worse while the operating room is readied

outcomes.story: He is moved to a ward bed for hourly checks. At the first check he cannot be woken. His left pupil is wide and does not react, and his breathing is slow and uneven.
outcomes.reply: Watching is for a small bleed in a patient who is awake and well. His is large, his brain is shifted, and he was already getting worse. An hour of watching nearly cost him his life. He goes to surgery now.
outcomes.alarm: Cannot be woken · left pupil fixed · slow, uneven breathing

outcomes.story: The antiseizure medicine runs in, and his blood pressure is brought down to normal. Forty minutes later he no longer opens his eyes, and his right side barely moves.
outcomes.reply: Neither of those removes the blood. And his high blood pressure was his body’s way of forcing blood into a squeezed brain. Lowering it took that away. He needs the clot out, now.
outcomes.alarm: No longer opens his eyes · blood pressure lowered

outcomes.story: You ask intensive care to start cooling him. The neurosurgeon overhears.
outcomes.reply: Cooling does not remove a clot. It would only delay the one thing that will save him. He is going to the operating room.

4.resident: The operating room needs a few more minutes. His left pupil is wider and his right side is weaker than when he was scanned. His brain is being squeezed downward.
4.question: How do we buy him those minutes?
options: Breathe for him very fast, and keep that up for hours
Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees, breathe for him a little faster for a short time, and give a strong salt solution or mannitol
Run in a large amount of dilute (hypotonic) fluid, fast
Bring his blood pressure down below 100 with nitroprusside
4.fix: Head up, brief faster breathing, salt solution

terms.meaning: The skull is a closed box. Blood, brain and fluid share the space, so extra blood raises the pressure on everything else.
A very salty solution given through a vein. It draws water out of the brain and into the blood.
Breathing off extra carbon dioxide narrows the brain’s blood vessels and lowers the pressure for a few minutes. Too much, or too long, starves the brain of blood.
High blood pressure with a slow pulse and slow breathing. It is the body’s last-ditch reaction to dangerous pressure in the skull.

outcomes.story: You ask the anesthetist to breathe for him as fast as possible, and to keep it going. The anesthetist says no.
outcomes.reply: A little faster, for a few minutes, narrows the brain’s blood vessels and eases the pressure. Much faster, for hours, narrows them so far that the brain is starved of blood. It is a brief bridge and nothing more.

outcomes.story: The head of the bed goes up, with his neck kept straight. A strong salt solution runs into a vein, and the anesthetist breathes for him a little faster for a few minutes. His left pupil comes down slightly. He is wheeled into the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Each of those eases the pressure a little: blood drains from the head more easily, the vessels narrow, and water is drawn out of the brain. Together they bought the minutes he needed. The surgery is what saves him.
outcomes.alarm: On the way to surgery · pressure eased for now

outcomes.story: You ask for two liters of dilute fluid, run in fast. The nurse reads the bag and checks with the resident.
outcomes.reply: Dilute fluid moves into brain cells and makes the brain swell. That is the opposite of what he needs. In a head injury we give salty fluids, never dilute ones.

outcomes.story: The nitroprusside runs in, and his blood pressure falls to 96 over 54. Within minutes he stops responding altogether.
outcomes.reply: His blood pressure was high on purpose. With that much pressure in his skull, a high blood pressure is the only thing pushing blood into his brain. Bringing it down cut off the supply. We stop the drip and treat the pressure in his skull.

differential.resident: The scan is in his chart. Look at the shape of the blood, and at where it stops.
differential.question: What kind of bleed is this?
options: Subdural hematoma: bleeding from torn veins, spread in a crescent over the brain
Epidural hematoma: bleeding from a torn artery, between the skull and the brain’s covering
Diffuse axonal injury: nerve fibers torn throughout the brain, with a nearly normal scan
Bleeding into the fluid spaces around the brain (subarachnoid hemorrhage)
A bruise within the brain tissue itself (contusion)
differential.reveal: It is an epidural hematoma. The blow cracked the thin bone at his temple and tore the artery that runs along its inner surface. Blood under arterial pressure peels the brain’s covering off the skull, which is why it bulges like a lens and stops at the skull’s seams. Being knocked out, waking up and then fading fast is the classic story.

terms.meaning: Outside the dura, the tough outer covering of the brain, and just under the skull.
A collection of blood outside the blood vessels.
An artery that runs in a groove on the inside of the skull at the temple, where the bone is thinnest.

ending.stable: In the operating room
ending.unstable: In the operating room, in time
ending.worse: In the operating room, after getting worse on the way
ending.critical: In the operating room, in critical condition

nr-016.plainDiagnosis: Bleeding from a torn artery between the skull and the brain’s covering (an epidural hematoma), pressing on the brain.

science.title: Why blood inside a closed box is deadly
science.text: The skull is rigid and closed. The blood collecting inside it has nowhere to go, so the pressure on everything else rises, and the soft brain is pushed sideways and downward.

science.title: Why his blood pressure was high and his pulse slow
science.text: Blood enters the brain only if the pressure pushing it in beats the pressure inside the skull. As that inside pressure climbed, his body drove his blood pressure up to keep blood flowing, and a reflex slowed his heart in response. Lowering his blood pressure would have cut the brain’s supply.

science.title: How a salty drip shrinks a swollen brain
science.text: Water moves across membranes toward the saltier side. A very salty solution in his blood draws water out of the brain tissue and into the vessels, so the brain takes up a little less room. Dilute fluid would do the reverse.

science.title: How a few fast breaths lower the pressure
science.text: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the blood forms an acid. Breathing faster blows it off, and the blood turns slightly less acidic. The brain’s blood vessels narrow in response and hold less blood, which frees a little room in the skull for a few minutes.

sources.title: Brain Trauma Foundation (2006): surgical management of acute epidural hematomas
Brain Trauma Foundation (2017): guidelines for the management of severe traumatic brain injury, fourth edition
Brain Trauma Foundation: guidelines for the surgical management of traumatic brain injury

nr-008.title: A drooping eyelid _after a neck adjustment._

start.alarm: Neck pain · right eyelid drooping

nr-008.handoff: A 38-year-old man has had pain in the right side of his neck and face for two days. It began the day after a chiropractor adjusted his neck. He has noticed that his right eyelid droops and his right pupil looks smaller.

interview.prompt: Ask when it started, and what happened to his neck beforehand
interview.finding: The pain in his right neck and face began the day after a chiropractor adjusted his neck for stiffness. The drooping eyelid and the smaller pupil appeared over the next two days.

interview.prompt: Ask about his eyes and his vision
interview.finding: He has seen in the mirror that his right eyelid droops and his right pupil is smaller. He has no double vision and no loss of vision.

interview.prompt: Ask about any passing symptoms, and his risks
interview.finding: His left hand tingled for a short while and then recovered. He has no weakness or slurred speech now. He is healthy and has never smoked.

exam.prompt: Look at his pupils, eyelids and eye movements
exam.finding: His right upper eyelid droops a little, and his right pupil is smaller than the left, though it still reacts to light. Sweating on his face looks normal. His eye movements, eyesight and side vision are normal.

exam.prompt: Do a full check of his nervous system
exam.finding: Apart from the eyelid and the pupil, everything is normal: speech, face, strength, sensation, coordination and walking.

exam.prompt: Examine his neck
exam.finding: The front of his neck on the right is tender. No whooshing sound is heard over the artery, and his heartbeat is regular.

2.label: Artery scan
2.content:
CT scan of the neck arteries with dye (CT angiogram): the right internal carotid artery narrows to a long, tapering point, like a flame. Its wall is thickened on one side by a crescent of blood, starting about 2 cm above the point where the artery forks.
CT scan of the brain: no bleeding and no stroke.
Heart tracing (ECG): a normal rhythm.

0.resident: Look at his right eye. The lid droops and the pupil is small. Those two findings together have a name.
0.question: Which pattern is this?
options: Third nerve palsy: a drooping lid with a large pupil, and an eye turned down and out
Horner syndrome: a drooping lid with a small pupil
Myasthenia gravis: lids that droop more as the day goes on, with double vision
Bell’s palsy: weakness of one whole side of the face

terms.meaning: The nerves that widen the pupil, lift the eyelid slightly and control sweating. They run a long route from the brain down to the chest and back up the neck to the eye.
A small pupil.
A drooping upper eyelid.

outcomes.story: You write “third nerve palsy” in his notes. The resident points at his pupil.
outcomes.reply: A third nerve palsy gives a large pupil, and the eye turns down and out. His pupil is small and his eye moves normally. A drooping lid with a small pupil is Horner syndrome.

outcomes.story: You name it, and the resident nods. You write it in his notes, with the neck pain underlined.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Horner syndrome means the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye has been interrupted somewhere along its route. Those nerves run up the neck wrapped around the carotid artery. With new neck pain after a neck adjustment, the artery is where we look.

outcomes.story: You write “myasthenia gravis?” in his notes. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: Myasthenia makes the lids droop more with tiredness, and causes double vision. It never changes the pupil. His pupil is small, so this is Horner syndrome.

outcomes.story: You write “Bell’s palsy” in his notes. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Bell’s palsy weakens the muscles of one side of the face: the smile, the forehead, closing the eye. It does not make the lid droop like this or shrink the pupil. This is Horner syndrome.

1.resident: Horner syndrome with new neck pain, the day after his neck was adjusted. I am worried about a tear in the wall of his carotid artery.
1.question: Which test will show it?
options: A CT or MRI scan of the arteries in his head and neck
A plain CT scan of his head only
A spinal tap
A blood test for myasthenia gravis antibodies

terms.meaning: One of the two large arteries in the front of the neck that carry blood to the brain.
A scan that outlines the arteries, using dye for CT or a magnet for MRI. It shows both the channel and the wall.
A tear in an artery’s inner lining that lets blood track into the wall. Clots can form there and travel to the brain.

outcomes.story: He goes for a CT scan with dye that outlines the arteries from his chest to his brain. A plain scan of the brain and a heart tracing are done on the same visit. The report goes in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. We need to see the wall of the artery and the channel inside it, and this scan shows both.

outcomes.story: The plain head CT is normal, and you tell him so. While he waits to be sent home, his left hand goes numb and clumsy for ten minutes, then recovers.
outcomes.reply: A plain head CT shows the brain. It cannot show the wall of an artery in the neck, so a normal result told us nothing about a tear. That spell in his hand was most likely a small clot from the artery reaching his brain. He needs the artery scan now.
outcomes.alarm: Left hand went numb and clumsy for ten minutes

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: A spinal tap looks for infection or bleeding around the brain. Nothing here suggests either, and it would tell us nothing about an artery.

outcomes.story: You send blood for myasthenia antibodies. The resident cancels the request.
outcomes.reply: Myasthenia does not cause a small pupil or neck pain. The result would take days and would not explain him. The artery cannot wait.

4.resident: The scan confirms a tear in the wall of his right carotid artery. His brain scan is clear. A clot can form on the torn wall and travel to the brain, and his left hand has already given one warning.
4.question: How do we protect him?
options: Start a medicine to prevent clots (an antiplatelet drug or a blood thinner), and no more neck adjustments
Emergency surgery to clean out the artery (carotid endarterectomy)
High-dose steroids
No treatment: reassure him and send him home

terms.meaning: Any medicine that prevents clots. Antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin make platelets less sticky. Anticoagulants slow the clotting proteins.
The specialists who decide on treatment to prevent or treat a stroke.
An operation that removes fatty plaque from inside the carotid artery. It is for narrowing caused by plaque.

outcomes.story: The stroke team reviews him, checks for any reason he should not have a clot-preventing medicine, and starts one. He is admitted to the stroke unit for regular checks. He is told plainly: no more neck adjustments.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment. The medicine keeps clots from forming on the torn wall while it heals over the coming months. Whether to use an antiplatelet drug or a blood thinner is a choice the stroke team makes for each patient.

outcomes.story: You call the vascular surgeons to book the operation. The surgeon asks what the scan showed, then declines.
outcomes.reply: That operation scrapes out fatty plaque. He has no plaque. He has a tear in a fragile wall, and cutting into it would make things worse. Tears like this are treated with medicine, and most heal.

outcomes.story: You write for high-dose steroids. The resident reads the order.
outcomes.reply: Steroids treat inflamed arteries, as in giant cell arteritis. His artery is torn, not inflamed. Steroids would do nothing for it.

outcomes.story: You start to tell him it will settle on its own. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: The pain may settle. The danger does not. A torn neck artery is one of the main causes of stroke in young adults, and the risk is highest in the first few weeks. He does not go home without treatment and a plan.

5.resident: He has a good question. His eyelid droops and his pupil is small, but the right side of his face still sweats normally. He wants to know why.
5.question: What do we tell him?
options: Because the first nerve cell on the route, the one inside the brain, is undamaged
Because the sweat fibers for the face follow a different artery, the external carotid, so a tear in the internal carotid spares them
Because Horner syndrome never affects sweating
Because the damaged fibers are parasympathetic ones

terms.meaning: The carotid artery forks in the neck. The internal branch goes to the brain and the eye. The external branch supplies the face and scalp.
A drooping lid and a small pupil with normal sweating on the face. It points to a problem along the internal carotid artery.
The nerves that narrow the pupil. They are the counterpart to the sympathetic nerves that widen it.

outcomes.story: You tell him the first nerve cell on the route was spared. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It was spared, but that is not why he sweats. The reason is further along. In the neck the fibers split up: the ones for sweating on the face follow the external carotid artery, and his tear is in the internal carotid.

outcomes.story: You draw the fork in the artery for him. The sweat fibers go one way, and the fibers for the eye go the other, along the artery that tore. He nods.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. That is why a drooping lid and a small pupil with normal sweating points straight at the internal carotid artery. The pattern itself tells you where the damage is.

outcomes.story: You tell him Horner syndrome never affects sweating. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: It often does. When the damage is lower down, in the brain, the spinal cord or the chest, that side of the face stops sweating too. His sweating is spared because of where his damage is.

outcomes.story: You tell him his parasympathetic fibers are damaged. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Those are the fibers that make the pupil smaller, and his are working. That is the point: with the sympathetic supply cut, nothing opposes them, so the pupil stays small.

differential.resident: The artery scan is in his chart. Look at the shape of the narrowing, and at the wall.
differential.question: What does he have?
options: Carotid narrowing from fatty plaque (atherosclerosis)
A tear in the wall of the internal carotid artery (carotid dissection)
A growth at the fork of the carotid artery (carotid body tumor)
An inflamed artery (giant cell arteritis)
differential.reveal: It is a carotid dissection. Blood has tracked into the wall of his right internal carotid artery, which gives the long, flame-shaped narrowing and the crescent in the wall. Plaque sits at the fork of the artery, in older people. A tear like this can follow minor strain on the neck, and a neck adjustment is a recognized trigger.

terms.meaning: Blood trapped within the wall of an artery.
Fatty plaque that builds up in artery walls over decades.

ending.stable: In the stroke unit on a clot-preventing medicine
ending.worse: In the stroke unit on a clot-preventing medicine, after a second warning spell
ending.critical: In the stroke unit after a stroke

nr-008.plainDiagnosis: A tear in the wall of the right carotid artery in the neck (carotid dissection), which cut off part of the nerve supply to his eye.

science.title: Why a tear in the wall threatens the brain
science.text: Blood trapped in the artery’s wall bulges inward and narrows the channel. Flow is disturbed as it passes the damaged lining, and platelets stick there. A clot that breaks free is carried straight up to the brain.

science.title: How either medicine would protect him
science.text: Both kinds of medicine he might be given work on enzymes. Aspirin switches off an enzyme that platelets need in order to clump. Blood thinners block enzymes in the chain that builds a clot. Either way, a clot is less likely to form on the torn wall.

sources.title: AHA scientific statement (2024): treatment and outcomes of cervical artery dissection in adults
CADISS trial (Lancet Neurol 2015): antiplatelet treatment versus anticoagulation for cervical artery dissection
TREAT-CAD trial (Lancet Neurol 2021): aspirin versus anticoagulation in cervical artery dissection

nr-101.title: She went stiff, _then began to shake._
nr-101.handoff: A 31-year-old woman became unresponsive while sitting down. Her partner saw her stiffen and jerk on both sides for about 90 seconds. She was confused for 15 minutes afterward. She is back to normal now.

interview.prompt: Ask her partner what the movements looked like, and how she recovered
interview.finding: Both sides of her body stiffened and then jerked for about 90 seconds. She was confused for about 15 minutes afterward. Her partner did not see the very first seconds clearly.

interview.prompt: Ask about triggers and anything that could have set it off
interview.finding: She was sitting, not standing, and had no warm, sweaty warning. She has had no fever, no head injury and no alcohol withdrawal. Nothing like this has happened before.

interview.prompt: Ask how she feels now
interview.finding: She feels back to normal. She has no lasting headache, and no weakness, numbness or trouble speaking.

exam.prompt: Check her thinking and her nervous system
exam.finding: She knows where she is and what day it is. Her strength, sensation, speech and coordination are normal, and her neck is not stiff.

exam.prompt: Look for injuries
exam.finding: There is a small bite on the side of her tongue. She has no significant head injury.

exam.prompt: Listen to her heart and check her pulse
exam.finding: Her pulse is regular, there is no murmur, and her vital signs are steady.

1.label: First checks
1.content:
Her partner’s detailed account confirms a long confused spell afterward, and the bite is on the side of her tongue.
Blood sugar: 94, normal. Blood salts: no relevant upset.
Heart tracing (ECG): a normal rhythm, with no problem reported in the timing or shape of the signals.
No immediate cause has been found. That is not proof that every cause has been ruled out.

4.label: Brain-wave test and follow-up
4.content:
A routine brain-wave test (EEG), done while she was awake, showed no seizure-type activity.
She has had no second event.
The specialist assessment is still under way.

0.resident: She has recovered and she is safe. Before anyone puts a label on this, we need the basics.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: Book an MRI as an outpatient, and classify the event from how the shaking looked
Watch her for another event before doing any tests
Ask for an urgent brain-wave test (EEG), and hold everything else until it is reported
Go over what her partner saw, examine her, check her blood sugar and salts, and get a heart tracing (ECG)
0.fix: Story, exam, blood tests and ECG

terms.meaning: What someone saw before, during and after an event. It is often the most useful clue there is.
A tracing of the heart’s electrical signals. Some heart rhythm problems cause blackouts with jerking that look like seizures.
To put a precise label on an event, such as where in the brain a seizure began. A label given too early can be wrong, and hard to remove.

outcomes.story: You book an MRI for next month and write “generalized seizure” in her notes. The resident reads the note.
outcomes.reply: Shaking on both sides does not tell us where it started, and her partner missed the first seconds. A scan next month also skips the checks she needs today. We start with the story, the exam, blood tests and a heart tracing.

outcomes.story: You plan to keep her on a monitor and wait for another event. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: She may not have another for months, or ever. The event she has already had is reason enough to assess her now, while her partner’s memory is fresh.

outcomes.story: You request an urgent EEG and put everything else on hold. The resident reads the request.
outcomes.reply: An EEG has its place, but a normal one would not rule a seizure out, and it cannot find a heart cause or a chemical one. Those are quick to check and dangerous to miss.

outcomes.story: You sit with her partner and go through the event second by second. You examine her, a fingerstick sugar and blood tests are done, and a heart tracing is recorded. The findings go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Good. The account is the most useful test we have. The heart tracing matters because some rhythm problems cause blackouts with jerking, and those can kill.

3.resident: This looks like a first seizure. We do not know where in the brain it began, or why. Her first checks are reassuring.
3.question: What is the plan from here?
options: Give safety advice, and ask for a specialist only if it happens again
Book a routine EEG as an outpatient, then decide whether she needs a specialist
Arrange an urgent first-seizure assessment with a specialist, give safety advice for the meantime, and order the tests that are indicated
Start a daily antiseizure medicine, and book a routine visit once the dose is settled

terms.meaning: A prompt visit with a specialist who takes the full story, examines the patient and decides which tests and treatment, if any, are needed.
What to do, and what to avoid, until the specialist visit: for example, not swimming or bathing alone, and what others should do if it happens again.
Tests chosen because of what the story and the examination show, not ordered by routine.

outcomes.story: You give her a safety leaflet and tell her to come back if it happens again. The resident stops her at the door.
outcomes.reply: Waiting for a second seizure means the next one may happen on the stairs or in the bath. After a first suspected seizure she should see a specialist promptly. The pathway we follow aims for within two weeks.

outcomes.story: You book a routine EEG and plan to decide afterward. The resident reads the plan.
outcomes.reply: An EEG cannot decide this. It is normal in many people with epilepsy, so a normal result would wrongly end the matter. The specialist sees her first, and chooses the tests.

outcomes.story: You make the urgent referral, and she is given an appointment within two weeks. You go through the safety advice with her and her partner: what to do if it happens again, who to call, and what to avoid for now. The tests the specialist will want are requested.
outcomes.reply: Right. She gets expert eyes on this quickly, and she is safer in the meantime. Whether she needs any long-term treatment is decided at that visit, not today.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for a daily antiseizure medicine. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: We do not know yet what this was, or why it happened. A daily medicine is a long-term decision with side effects, and it is made with a specialist after a proper assessment.

5.resident: Her routine EEG has come back normal. She has had no second event, and the specialist assessment is still going on.
5.question: What does the normal EEG change?
options: Epilepsy is still possible: read the EEG together with the story and the rest of the assessment
A simple faint is now the leading explanation: switch her follow-up to a heart and circulation check
Her risk of another event is now low enough to lift the safety advice
A functional seizure is now the leading explanation: arrange a psychological assessment

terms.meaning: About half an hour of brain-wave recording. It samples a short window, and can easily miss activity that comes and goes.
An event that looks like a seizure but is not caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It is a real condition, and it is diagnosed on positive evidence.
A test good enough that a normal result rules a condition out. A routine EEG is not one.

outcomes.story: You explain to her that a normal recording is good news, but only a short sample. Her safety advice stays in place, and the specialist will decide whether any further recording is needed.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. Many people with epilepsy have a normal routine EEG. The story still carries the most weight, and it has not changed.

outcomes.story: You rewrite her follow-up as a heart check for fainting. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: A normal EEG does not turn a seizure into a faint. Her event had none of a faint’s features: she was sitting, she had no warning, and she was confused for 15 minutes afterward. The plan stays as it was.

outcomes.story: You tell her she can drop the precautions. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: A normal EEG does not make another event unlikely. The precautions exist for the chance of a second one, and that chance has not gone away.

outcomes.story: You refer her for a psychological assessment. The resident stops the referral.
outcomes.reply: A functional seizure is diagnosed from positive findings, not because a test came back normal. Nothing in her story points that way, and a normal EEG does not either.

differential.resident: Her first checks are in the chart. Be careful how much you claim.
differential.question: What is the best way to describe this event right now?
options: A simple faint that came with some jerking
A first suspected seizure, with its starting point and its cause not yet known
A first generalized tonic-clonic seizure, as part of a generalized epilepsy syndrome
A functional seizure that needs a specialist in non-epileptic events
differential.reveal: The best description is a first suspected seizure, with where it started and why still unknown. The long confusion afterward and the bite on the side of her tongue support a seizure. Jerking on both sides does not show where it began, and one event does not make an epilepsy syndrome. Normal first checks do not make it a functional event, either.

terms.meaning: Likely enough to act on, but not proven.
Involving both sides of the brain from the start. That cannot be judged when the first seconds were not seen.
A recognized pattern of seizures, age and test findings. One event is not enough to diagnose one.

ending.stable: Going home with safety advice, with the specialist assessment under way
ending.worse: Kept in for observation
ending.critical: In the resuscitation room

nr-101.plainDiagnosis: A first suspected seizure. Where in the brain it began, and why, are not yet known.

science.title: Why a normal test did not close the question
science.text: A routine EEG records about half an hour of brain activity. In many people with epilepsy the telltale activity comes and goes, so a short recording often misses it. A test that often misses a condition cannot be used to rule it out.

science.title: Why a heart tracing was part of a brain workup
science.text: The brain needs a constant supply of blood. If a heart rhythm fault stops the pump for a few seconds, the brain shuts down and the body can stiffen and jerk, which looks like a seizure. Her tracing showed a normal rhythm.

science.title: Why her blood sugar was checked
science.text: Nerve cells run on glucose and store almost none. A very low blood sugar can set off a seizure, and it is fixed in minutes once it is found. Hers was a normal 94.

sources.title: NICE NG217: epilepsies in children, young people and adults, diagnosis and assessment
NICE CG109: transient loss of consciousness, initial assessment
AAN/AES practice parameter (2007): evaluating an apparent unprovoked first seizure in adults
ILAE official report (2014): a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

ns-006.title: Numb, and _unable to pass urine._

start.alarm: Cannot pass urine · numb between the legs

ns-006.handoff: A 35-year-old woman hurt her back moving furniture two days ago. The pain now runs down both legs. Since this morning she has been numb between her legs and has not been able to pass urine.

interview.prompt: Ask about the back and leg pain
interview.finding: Severe low back pain for two days, since she moved furniture. It now shoots down both legs.

interview.prompt: Ask about her bladder, her bowels and the feeling between her legs
interview.finding: She has not passed urine since this morning and feels no urge to. Earlier she could not empty her bladder fully. She is numb between her legs and when she wipes, and she has become constipated.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever, weight loss and other risks
interview.finding: No fever and no weight loss. She does not inject drugs and has no immune problem. She has had back pain on and off for years.

exam.prompt: Test the feeling around her bottom and the muscle tone there
exam.finding: A pinprick feels dull over the area that would touch a saddle. The ring of muscle at her anus is slack, and the reflex that should tighten it is missing.

exam.prompt: Test her leg strength and reflexes
exam.finding: Lifting either straight leg sends pain shooting down it. Both ankle reflexes are weak, and her feet are slightly weak. There are no signs of damage to the spinal cord higher up.

exam.prompt: Feel her belly and her spine
exam.finding: Her bladder can be felt above her pubic bone, full and swollen. Her lower spine is tender. She has no fever.

1.label: Bladder scan and MRI
1.content:
Bladder scan after she tried to pass urine: 650 mL still inside. Normally very little is left.
MRI of the lower spine: a large slipped disc in the middle of the spine, between the fourth and fifth lumbar bones. It is squeezing the bundle of nerves that runs below the end of the spinal cord.
No abscess, tumor or bleed.
Feeling around her anus is reduced, and the muscle tone there is low.

0.resident: Back pain with numbness between the legs and a bladder that will not empty is an emergency until proven otherwise.
0.question: What do we do right now?
options: Give anti-inflammatory tablets and book physical therapy
Scan her bladder after she tries to pass urine, and get an emergency MRI of her lower spine
Get plain X-rays of her lower back, and send her home with advice
Get a CT scan of her head

terms.meaning: Loss of feeling in the area that would touch a saddle: the inner thighs, the genitals and around the anus. It means the lowest spinal nerves are in trouble.
A bladder that fills but cannot empty. When the nerves fail, it is often painless.
A scan that uses a magnet to show soft tissues such as discs and nerves, which X-rays cannot show.

outcomes.story: You write a prescription for anti-inflammatories and a physical therapy referral. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: That is the plan for ordinary back pain. Numbness between the legs and a bladder that will not empty mean the nerves to her bladder and bowel are being crushed. She cannot go home.

outcomes.story: The nurse scans her bladder after she tries to pass urine, and a catheter is put in to drain it. She is taken for an MRI within the hour. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The bladder scan puts a number on the nerve damage, and the MRI shows what is pressing on the nerves. Every hour counts here.

outcomes.story: The X-rays look normal, and you start her discharge papers. While she waits she leaks urine without feeling it, and when she stands her feet are weaker than before.
outcomes.reply: X-rays show bones. They cannot show a disc pressing on nerves, so normal films mean nothing here. She has lost an hour, and her nerves are worse for it. She needs the MRI now.
outcomes.alarm: Leaking urine without feeling it · feet weaker

outcomes.story: You request a CT of her head. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: Her brain is not the problem. Leg pain, saddle numbness and a failed bladder all point to the nerves at the bottom of the spine.

3.resident: The MRI shows a large disc crushing the nerves at the bottom of her spine. Her bladder was holding 650 mL.
3.question: What will fix this?
options: High-dose steroids through a vein, and watch her
Antibiotics through a vein
Emergency surgery to take the pressure off the nerves
A steroid injection into the spine, at a clinic in two weeks

terms.meaning: Surgery that removes whatever is pressing on nerves. Here that means part of the bone at the back of the spine, and the slipped disc.
The bundle of nerves that hangs below the end of the spinal cord. It serves the legs, the bladder, the bowel and sexual function.
The soft center of a spinal disc bulging out through its outer ring.

outcomes.story: The steroids run in and you watch her. Two hours later the numbness has spread down the backs of her thighs, and she can barely lift her feet.
outcomes.reply: Steroids do not move a disc. The nerves are still being crushed, and they are failing while we watch. Only surgery takes the pressure off. She goes now.

outcomes.story: You write for antibiotics. The pharmacist calls to ask what infection is being treated.
outcomes.reply: Antibiotics treat an abscess in the spine, and the MRI showed none. Her problem is mechanical: a disc pressing on nerves.

outcomes.story: The spine surgeon sees her straight away and books the operating room. She signs the consent form and is taken up.
outcomes.reply: Yes. This is one of the few true emergencies in spine surgery. The sooner the pressure comes off, the better her chance of getting bladder and bowel control back.

outcomes.story: You start a referral for a spinal injection in two weeks. The resident takes the form.
outcomes.reply: In two weeks the damage could be permanent. Injections ease pain from an irritated nerve. They do not lift a disc off nerves that are being crushed.

4.resident: Her partner asks whether the operation could wait until things settle down. What we say next has to be accurate.
4.question: What is true about timing?
options: Surgery can safely wait several weeks, because the damage is already done
Once the bladder has stopped working, surgery has nothing to offer
Surgery should wait until feeling starts to come back by itself
The sooner the pressure is taken off, the better the recovery of bladder, bowel and leg function, so surgery should not wait

terms.meaning: The likely outcome.
Nerves that have been squeezed can recover once the pressure is off, but less so the longer they were squeezed.

outcomes.story: You tell her partner it could wait a few weeks. The resident steps in.
outcomes.reply: The damage is still happening. Every hour of pressure makes permanent loss of bladder and bowel control more likely. It cannot wait weeks.

outcomes.story: You say that surgery will not help now that her bladder has failed. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: That is not so. Taking the pressure off can still bring function back, or stop it getting worse, even after the bladder has stopped working. It is still worth doing, and soon.

outcomes.story: You suggest waiting to see whether feeling returns. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: It will not return while the disc is still pressing on the nerves. The cause is mechanical, and it gets worse with time.

outcomes.story: You explain it to them both, and the resident nods. She is wheeled to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. How well she recovers depends on how bad things were when she arrived, and on how fast the pressure comes off. We can only change the second one.

differential.resident: The bladder scan and the MRI are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Cauda equina syndrome: the nerve bundle at the bottom of the spine is being crushed
A stroke of the lower end of the spinal cord
Inflammation across the spinal cord (transverse myelitis)
Guillain-Barré syndrome: the immune system attacking the nerves, with weakness that climbs from the feet
differential.reveal: It is cauda equina syndrome. A large slipped disc is crushing the bundle of nerves below the end of the spinal cord. Those nerves run the bladder, the bowel and the feeling in the saddle area, which is why she is numb there and cannot pass urine. Her weak reflexes fit damage to nerves, not to the spinal cord itself.

terms.meaning: A set of findings that occur together.
The nerves as they leave the spine, before they branch out to the body.

ending.stable: In the operating room for emergency surgery on her spine
ending.worse: In the operating room, weaker than when she arrived
ending.critical: In intensive care

ns-006.plainDiagnosis: A slipped disc crushing the nerves at the bottom of the spine (cauda equina syndrome).

science.title: Why she could not feel her bladder filling
science.text: Stretch sensors in the bladder wall report fullness through the lowest spinal nerves, and the same nerves carry the order to empty. With those nerves crushed, the signal never arrived and the order never left. Her bladder held 650 mL and she felt no urge.

science.title: Why squeezed nerves stop working
science.text: A nerve carries signals by moving ions across its membrane, and the pumps that reset it after each signal need a steady blood supply. Pressure cuts that supply off. The fibers fall silent first and die later, which is why speed matters.

sources.title: Ahn et al. (Spine 2000): cauda equina syndrome secondary to lumbar disc herniation, a meta-analysis of surgical outcomes
Lavy et al. (BMJ 2009): cauda equina syndrome

ns-030.title: A boy with a shunt, _harder and harder to wake._

start.alarm: Very sleepy · eyes turned down · slow heart rate

ns-030.handoff: A 7-year-old boy has a shunt, a tube that drains extra fluid from his brain. He has had headaches and vomiting for two days. Today he is very sleepy, and his parents say his eyes keep looking down.

interview.prompt: Ask his parents how this has gone
interview.finding: Two days of headache that keeps getting worse, with repeated vomiting. Today he is very sleepy and hard to wake from naps, and his eyes seem to look downward.

interview.prompt: Ask about his shunt
interview.finding: He was born early and had bleeding in the brain that blocked its fluid drainage. The shunt was put in when he was a baby and was last repaired when he was 4. His parents say this looks like the last time it failed.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever, illness and injury
interview.finding: No fever, no stiff neck, no recent illness, no belly pain, no injury and no seizures.

exam.prompt: Check how awake he is, and watch his eyes
exam.finding: He wakes to your voice, but he is irritable and wants to keep his eyes shut. Both eyes are turned downward, and he cannot look up. His pupils are equal and react to light.

exam.prompt: Look at the back of his eyes, and press the shunt’s reservoir
exam.finding: The nerve at the back of each eye is starting to swell, a sign of pressure. The small bubble of the shunt behind his right ear is slow to press and slow to refill.

exam.prompt: Check his neck and his limbs
exam.finding: His neck is not stiff. He moves both arms and both legs equally.

1.label: CT scan and shunt X-rays
1.content:
CT scan of the head: the fluid spaces inside his brain are much larger than on his scan a year ago. The grooves on the surface of the brain are squeezed flat, and fluid is seeping into the tissue around the spaces.
Shunt X-rays: the tubing has come apart at the level of his collarbone.
Temperature and white blood cell count: normal, so infection is unlikely.

0.resident: A child with a shunt who is sleepy and vomiting has a blocked shunt until we prove otherwise. Look at his heart rate and his blood pressure, too.
0.question: What do we get first?
options: A spinal tap
A brain-wave test (EEG)
A CT scan of his head (or a quick MRI), and X-rays along the whole shunt
Reassure his parents and watch him
0.fix: Scan his head and X-ray the shunt

terms.meaning: A thin tube with a valve that drains extra fluid from the brain to the belly, where the body absorbs it.
Too much fluid in the spaces inside the brain. The pressure squeezes the brain against the skull.
X-rays of the skull, neck, chest and belly that follow the tubing from end to end, looking for a break or a kink.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: Never when the fluid in the brain is blocked. Draining from below could pull the brain downward and kill him. A spinal tap also tells us nothing about the shunt.

outcomes.story: You request a brain-wave test. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: That is a test for seizures, and he has had none. His sleepiness comes from pressure, and the test would cost time he does not have.

outcomes.story: He is taken for a quick CT, and X-rays are taken along the tubing from his head to his belly. The neurosurgeon is called while the pictures come up, and his scan from last year is put up beside the new one.
outcomes.reply: Right. The scan shows whether fluid is building up, once it is set beside his old one. The X-rays show whether the tubing is broken.

outcomes.story: You tell his parents it may be a stomach bug and that you will keep an eye on him. An hour later he is very hard to wake, and he vomits again without stirring.
outcomes.reply: A stomach bug does not turn a child’s eyes downward or slow his heart. Those are signs of pressure on the brain, and it has been rising for another hour. Scan him now.
outcomes.alarm: Very hard to wake · heart rate slowing

3.resident: The fluid spaces in his brain have ballooned since last year, and the tubing has come apart at his collarbone. The shunt is not draining.
3.question: What is the plan?
options: Send him home with anti-sickness medicine
Start antibiotics through a vein and send him home
Book an MRI as an outpatient in a week
Urgent surgery to repair the shunt, with a needle into the shunt’s reservoir to check it and let some fluid off
3.fix: Call the neurosurgeons for urgent repair

terms.meaning: An operation to repair or replace the part of a shunt that has failed.
A fine needle passed through the skin into the shunt’s reservoir. It measures the pressure, and it can let fluid out to buy time.
The pressure inside the skull.

outcomes.story: You start his discharge papers. The resident takes them out of your hand.
outcomes.reply: The vomiting is not from his stomach. It is from pressure in his head, and that pressure can kill him. He is going to the operating room, not home.

outcomes.story: You write for antibiotics and a discharge. The resident reads it.
outcomes.reply: He has no fever and a normal blood count, so infection is unlikely. Even if the shunt were infected, antibiotics would not mend a broken tube. He needs it repaired.

outcomes.story: You book an MRI for next week. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: We already know what is wrong, and he will not last a week like this. The pressure is rising now.

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon comes down, and the operating room is booked. While it is being readied he gets sleepier. His right pupil is now larger than his left, and his heart rate is falling.
outcomes.reply: That was the right plan, made quickly. But the pressure is rising faster than the room can be set up. He needs fluid let off right now.
outcomes.alarm: Right pupil larger · heart rate falling

4.resident: His right pupil is wide, his heart rate is 52 and he is barely rousable. His brain is being squeezed downward.
4.question: What do we do this minute?
options: Drain fluid at once, through the shunt’s reservoir or straight from the brain’s fluid space, with the neurosurgeon operating immediately
A spinal tap to let the pressure off
Give a triptan for the headache
Repeat the shunt X-rays first

terms.meaning: Part of the brain being forced downward by pressure. It crushes the centers that control breathing and the heart.
A slow heart rate with high blood pressure. It is the body’s last-ditch reaction to dangerous pressure in the skull.
The fluid-filled spaces inside the brain.

outcomes.story: The neurosurgeon slides a fine needle into the reservoir behind his ear, and fluid comes out under pressure. Within minutes his pupil comes down, his heart rate climbs and he stirs. He is taken straight to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: That is what saved him. Letting fluid off through the shunt dropped the pressure in seconds and bought the time to repair it properly.
outcomes.alarm: Pressure relieved · on the way to surgery

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The neurosurgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: With a blocked system, draining from below pulls the brain down through the base of the skull. The fluid has to come off from above, through the shunt or the brain’s own fluid space.

outcomes.story: You ask for a migraine medicine. The resident stares at you.
outcomes.reply: This is not a migraine. A wide pupil and a falling heart rate mean his brain is being crushed. Only draining fluid will help.

outcomes.story: He is wheeled to X-ray for another set of films. On the table he stops responding. Both pupils are wide, and his breathing is slow and uneven.
outcomes.reply: We already knew where the tube was broken. Those films cost him twenty minutes he did not have. Drain the fluid, now.

differential.resident: The scan and the shunt X-rays are in his chart. Set the new scan beside last year’s.
differential.question: What has gone wrong?
options: An infected shunt
A migraine
A shunt that has stopped working because the tubing has come apart
A stomach bug
differential.reveal: His shunt has failed. The tubing has come apart at his collarbone, so fluid can no longer drain, and it is building up inside his brain. No fever and a normal blood count make infection unlikely. The downward-turned eyes come from pressure on the part of the brainstem that moves the eyes upward.

terms.meaning: A break, blockage or disconnection in the shunt itself, as opposed to an infection.
Eyes forced to look downward. In a child with a shunt it is a sign of high pressure in the brain.

ending.stable: In the operating room having his shunt repaired, with the pressure off his brain
ending.unstable: In the operating room having his shunt repaired, with the pressure off his brain
ending.worse: In the operating room, after getting worse while he waited
ending.critical: In the operating room in critical condition, after the pressure was left too long

ns-030.plainDiagnosis: A broken shunt, with fluid building up and pressing on the brain (shunt malfunction with hydrocephalus).

science.title: Why a broken tube is an emergency
science.text: His brain makes fluid around the clock. With the drain broken, the fluid has nowhere to go inside a closed skull, so the pressure climbs and the brain is squeezed.

science.title: Why his heart slowed as he got worse
science.text: As the pressure in the skull rises, less blood can get in. The body pushes the blood pressure up to force blood through, and a reflex then slows the heart. A slow pulse with high blood pressure in a sleepy child is a late warning.

sources.title: Hanak et al. (Pediatr Neurosurg 2017): cerebrospinal fluid shunting complications in children
Yue et al. (J Neurosurg Pediatr 2015): test characteristics of quick brain MRI for shunt evaluation in children

ns-010.title: Half his body _stopped working._

start.alarm: Right side paralyzed · very high blood pressure

ns-010.handoff: A 58-year-old man was watching television an hour ago when his right side went weak, his speech slurred and a severe headache began. He has high blood pressure and stopped taking his tablets months ago.

interview.prompt: Ask his wife when it started and how it has gone
interview.finding: It came on all at once an hour ago, while he was sitting still: weakness down his right side, slurred speech and a severe headache. He has grown drowsy and vomited once. Nothing has improved.

interview.prompt: Ask about his blood pressure and his medicines
interview.finding: He has had high blood pressure for years and stopped both his tablets months ago. He also has diabetes, and he smokes a pack a day.

interview.prompt: Ask about blood thinners, injuries and drugs
interview.finding: He takes no blood thinners. He has had no fall and no blow to the head, and he uses no recreational drugs.

exam.prompt: Check how awake he is, and listen to his speech
exam.finding: He is drowsy but wakes when spoken to. His words are badly slurred.

exam.prompt: Test his strength, feeling and vision
exam.finding: His right face, arm and leg do not move, and he cannot feel touch on that side. He cannot see things to his right, and his eyes stay turned to the left. His right big toe turns up when the sole is stroked.

exam.prompt: Check his pupils, his neck and his head
exam.finding: His pupils are equal and react to light. His neck is not stiff, and there is no sign of a head injury.

1.label: CT scan and blood tests
1.content:
CT scan of the head: fresh blood deep in the left side of the brain, about 25 mL (a little under two tablespoons), with little swelling around it.
The brain has not been pushed off center, and its fluid spaces are open.
Clotting tests and platelets: normal.
Blood sugar: 168, raised. Blood salts: normal.
His stroke score is high, which means a severe loss of function.

0.resident: This is a stroke, and he arrived inside the time window for the clot-busting drug. But a stroke can be a blocked artery or a burst one, and the two look the same at the bedside.
0.question: What has to happen before any treatment?
options: Give the clot-busting drug right away, going by how bad his weakness is
An emergency CT scan of his head, to tell a blocked artery from a bleed
Start aspirin and clopidogrel
Do a spinal tap

terms.meaning: Sudden loss of brain function because an artery is blocked or has burst.
A medicine that dissolves the clot in a blocked artery. In a bleed it makes the bleeding worse.
A needle in the lower back to sample the fluid around the brain and spinal cord. It looks for infection or bleeding.

outcomes.story: You ask for the clot-busting drug. The pharmacist will not release it without a scan.
outcomes.reply: His headache, his vomiting and a blood pressure of 214 all raise the chance that this is a bleed. A clot-buster in a bleeding brain is a disaster. Nobody gets it before a scan.

outcomes.story: He goes straight to the scanner with the stroke team beside him. The pictures are up within minutes, and blood is sent for clotting tests.
outcomes.reply: Right. The scan takes minutes and it decides everything, because the two kinds of stroke need opposite treatments.

outcomes.story: You write for aspirin and clopidogrel. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: Those make platelets less sticky. That helps when an artery is blocked, and it harms when one has burst. We do not know yet which this is.

outcomes.story: You ask for a spinal tap tray. The resident stops you.
outcomes.reply: A spinal tap answers nothing here, and it is dangerous if a large bleed is pressing on the brain. The scan comes first.

3.resident: The scan shows a bleed deep in the left side of his brain. His clotting is normal, and his blood pressure is still 214 over 118.
3.question: What is the core of his treatment?
options: The clot-busting drug, now
A full-dose blood thinner
Bring his blood pressure down in a controlled way, to a top number of about 130 to 140, watch his breathing and brain function closely, and correct any clotting problem
A drain placed in his lower back

terms.meaning: The bleed getting bigger in the first hours. It is the main reason patients get worse early.
Bringing blood pressure down with a medicine through a vein that can be adjusted minute by minute, without letting it crash.
Regular checks of wakefulness, pupils, speech and strength, to catch a change early.

outcomes.story: You ask for the clot-busting drug. The stroke team says no.
outcomes.reply: That drug dissolves clots. In a bleed, the clot is the only thing plugging the hole. It is ruled out completely.

outcomes.story: You write for a blood thinner. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: A blood thinner would make the bleed bigger. In a bleeding brain we want clotting to be as normal as it can be.

outcomes.story: A blood pressure medicine is started through a vein and adjusted every few minutes. Over the hour his top number comes down to 148. He is moved to the brain intensive care unit, where his wakefulness, pupils and strength are checked every fifteen minutes. A neurosurgeon reviews the scan.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment. High pressure pushes more blood out of the torn vessel, so we bring it down, steadily and not too far. Then we watch for the bleed growing or the pressure in his skull rising.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure coming down · checks every 15 minutes

outcomes.story: You ask for a drain in his lower back. The neurosurgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: Draining fluid from below, with a mass of blood above, risks pulling the brain downward. It is not a treatment for this.

4.resident: His family asks why the surgeons are not operating to take the blood out.
4.question: What is the honest answer?
options: Because surgery is not possible anywhere in the brain
Because deep bleeds never cause symptoms
Because medicines reliably dissolve the clot within hours
Because reaching a deep bleed means cutting through healthy brain, and for most patients it has not been shown to help, so surgery is kept for selected cases
4.fix: Explain why surgery is held back

terms.meaning: Clusters of nerve cells deep in the brain that help control movement.
For example, a large bleed in the cerebellum at the back of the brain, or one squeezing the brainstem, or a patient who is getting worse from a clot the surgeon can reach.

outcomes.story: You tell them brain surgery is not possible. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Brain surgery is done every day. The real reason is that this bleed is deep, and reaching it means cutting through healthy brain, which has not been shown to help most patients.

outcomes.story: You tell them deep bleeds do not cause symptoms. The resident looks at the patient, then at you.
outcomes.reply: He cannot move half his body. Deep bleeds cause severe symptoms. Surgery is held back because reaching the clot means cutting through healthy brain, with no proven benefit for most patients.

outcomes.story: You tell them the medicines will dissolve the clot. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: No medicine dissolves this clot. The body clears it slowly, over weeks. Our treatment stops it growing. Surgery is held back because, for most patients, reaching it does more harm than good.

outcomes.story: You explain it to his family. The resident adds that the neurosurgeon is still watching him, in case that changes.
outcomes.reply: That is accurate, and kind. In trials, routinely operating on bleeds like his did not improve outcomes. If he gets worse, or if the bleed were somewhere a surgeon could reach safely, the answer could change.

differential.resident: The scan is in his chart. Look at where the blood is, and remember his blood pressure.
differential.question: What kind of stroke is this?
options: A bleed deep in the brain from long-standing high blood pressure
A blocked artery (ischemic stroke)
A burst aneurysm bleeding around the brain (subarachnoid hemorrhage)
A brain abscess
differential.reveal: It is a bleed deep in the brain, caused by years of high blood pressure. The pressure weakens the tiny arteries that feed the deep parts of the brain until one bursts. A blocked artery shows no fresh blood on the scan. A burst aneurysm bleeds around the brain, not into the middle of it.

terms.meaning: Bleeding into the brain tissue itself.
Caused by high blood pressure.

ending.stable: In the brain intensive care unit with his blood pressure controlled
ending.unstable: In the brain intensive care unit with his blood pressure controlled, being watched closely
ending.worse: In the brain intensive care unit, after getting worse
ending.critical: In the brain intensive care unit in critical condition

ns-010.plainDiagnosis: Bleeding deep in the left side of the brain from long-standing high blood pressure (hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage).

science.title: Why years of high pressure burst a small artery
science.text: The deep parts of the brain are fed by tiny arteries that branch straight off large ones, so they take close to the full force of each heartbeat. Years of high pressure damage their thin walls until one gives way.

science.title: Why lowering his pressure limits the bleed
science.text: Blood leaves a torn vessel faster when the pressure behind it is higher. Bringing his blood pressure down slows the leak and gives a clot the chance to seal the tear. Lowering it too far, too fast, would starve the rest of the brain.

sources.title: 2022 AHA/ASA guideline: management of patients with spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage
INTERACT2 trial (NEJM 2013): rapid blood-pressure lowering in acute intracerebral hemorrhage
STICH II trial (Lancet 2013): early surgery versus initial conservative treatment in lobar intracerebral hematomas

gs-023.title: The worst pain _he has ever felt._

start.alarm: Severe constant pain · fast heart rate · fever

gs-023.handoff: A 66-year-old man has had severe belly pain for eight hours, and it keeps getting worse. He is vomiting and has passed nothing since it began. He had an abdominal operation 20 years ago.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain
interview.finding: It came on suddenly eight hours ago. It is severe, all over his belly and constant. He has had crampy belly pain before that came and went, and he says this is different: it never lets up. He is vomiting green fluid.

interview.prompt: Ask about his bowels
interview.finding: He has passed no stool and no gas since the pain began.

interview.prompt: Ask about past operations and medicines
interview.finding: He had an operation on his abdomen for a stab wound 20 years ago, and a groin hernia repaired long ago. He takes tablets for blood pressure and cholesterol.

exam.prompt: Look at his belly and press on it
exam.finding: His belly is swollen. The middle is very tender, and the muscles there tighten against your hand without him meaning to. Letting go quickly hurts him more. Few bowel sounds can be heard.

exam.prompt: Check for a hernia, and examine his rectum
exam.finding: There is no bulge in either groin or along his old scar. His rectum is empty, with no blood.

exam.prompt: Check his skin and how alert he is
exam.finding: He was restless and is now drowsy and slightly confused. His knees are cool and blotchy.

1.label: Blood tests and CT scan
1.content:
White blood cells: 18.4, high.
Lactate: 4.8 and rising (it was 3.1). Lactate builds up when tissue is starved of oxygen.
Kidney tests: mildly raised, a sign that he is short of fluid.
CT scan: two swollen loops of small bowel that meet at a single point, where the blood vessels are twisted into a whirl. The wall of the trapped loop is not taking up dye, which means little blood is reaching it. A small amount of free fluid.

0.resident: Scar tissue from an old operation can block the bowel. Most of those blockages settle without surgery. Something here tells me this one will not.
0.question: What sets him apart from a simple blockage?
options: He is vomiting green fluid
Constant, severe pain that is far worse than his belly looks, with fever, a fast heart rate and guarding
He has had an abdominal operation before
He has passed no gas for hours

terms.meaning: A blockage of the bowel. Food, fluid and gas cannot get past it.
A trapped piece of bowel whose blood supply is being cut off. Without blood it dies within hours.
Belly muscles that tighten by reflex when the lining of the abdomen is inflamed.

outcomes.story: You point to the green vomit. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Any blockage of the small bowel causes that. It tells us there is a blockage, not how dangerous it is.

outcomes.story: You tell the resident what worries you. Blood is drawn, fluids are started and he is sent for a CT scan. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. Crampy pain that comes and goes is a simple blockage. Constant pain with fever and a racing heart means the bowel itself is in trouble.

outcomes.story: You point to his old operation. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That explains why he has a blockage, because old scar tissue is the usual cause. It does not tell us whether this one is simple or dangerous.

outcomes.story: You point out that he has passed no gas. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That happens in any complete blockage. Look at the pain, the fever and his heart rate instead.

3.resident: The scan shows a trapped, twisted loop with almost no blood reaching it. His lactate is climbing.
3.question: What do we do?
options: Pass a tube through his nose to empty the stomach, and wait 48 hours
Fluids and antibiotics through a vein now, and straight to the operating room
Give a contrast drink and see whether it passes through
Admit him, examine his belly every few hours and repeat the lactate in 12 hours
3.fix: Call the surgeon and get him to the operating room

terms.meaning: An operation that opens the abdomen so the surgeon can see and fix the problem.
A substance cells make when they run short of oxygen. A rising level is a warning.
A hole in the bowel wall. Bowel contents leak into the abdomen and cause severe infection.

outcomes.story: The tube goes down and he is admitted to wait. Two hours later his belly is hard all over, and his blood pressure is falling.
outcomes.reply: Waiting works for a simple blockage. His bowel has no blood supply, and it has been dying for two more hours. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Belly hard all over · blood pressure falling

outcomes.story: Fluids run in fast and antibiotics are given. The surgeon sees him within minutes, and he is taken to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Right. Fluids and antibiotics buy a little time, and only an operation can untwist the loop. Every hour of waiting costs him bowel.

outcomes.story: You ask for the contrast drink. The surgeon cancels it.
outcomes.reply: That test is for a simple blockage, to see whether it will open by itself. With a strangled loop it only wastes time.

outcomes.story: He is admitted for checks every few hours. By the time anyone looks closely again, four hours have passed. He is cold and confused, and his belly is rigid.
outcomes.reply: A strangled loop does not wait twelve hours. Part of his bowel has died, and he is now in shock. He goes to the operating room this minute.

4.resident: You are watching in the operating room. The surgeon cuts a band of scar tissue and frees the loop. Twenty minutes later the loop is still dark, limp and not moving.
4.question: What should happen to that loop?
options: Put it back and close the abdomen
Cut out the dead segment and join the healthy ends, or plan a second look if it is borderline
Wrap it in warm packs for two more hours, then close whatever it looks like
Leave it in place and build a bypass around it
4.fix: Say it has to come out

terms.meaning: Alive and able to recover. Healthy bowel is pink and shiny, and it moves.
Cutting out a damaged piece of bowel.
Joining two cut ends of bowel so that it is one tube again.

outcomes.story: You suggest putting it back. The surgeon answers without looking up.
outcomes.reply: Dead bowel left inside breaks down and leaks within days. It has to come out.

outcomes.story: The surgeon removes the dead segment and joins the two healthy ends. The rest of the bowel is pink and moving.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Bowel that stays dark and still after its blood supply is restored will not recover. When the surgeon is unsure, they look again a day or two later.

outcomes.story: You suggest warming it for two more hours. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Twenty minutes is long enough to see whether it will recover. Closing over bowel that is still dark means closing over dead tissue.

outcomes.story: You suggest a bypass. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: A bypass would leave dead bowel inside as a source of infection. It has to be removed.

differential.resident: The blood tests and the scan are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A simple partial blockage from scar tissue
A trapped, twisted loop of bowel that is losing its blood supply (closed-loop obstruction with strangulation)
A colon that has swollen without any blockage
A bowel that has stopped moving, without any blockage (ileus)
differential.reveal: A loop of his small bowel is trapped at two points by a band of scar tissue and has twisted on its own blood supply. The whirl of vessels on the scan is that twist, and the wall that takes up no dye is bowel with no blood reaching it. A simple blockage would still have a healthy blood supply.

terms.meaning: A length of bowel blocked at both ends, so nothing can get in or out and pressure builds inside.
A band of scar tissue inside the abdomen, usually left by an earlier operation.

ending.stable: Recovering in intensive care after surgery, with the dead bowel removed
ending.unstable: Recovering in intensive care after surgery, with the dead bowel removed
ending.worse: In intensive care after surgery, sicker than he needed to be
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support, after an operation that came late

gs-023.plainDiagnosis: A trapped, twisted loop of small bowel that had lost its blood supply (closed-loop obstruction with strangulation).

science.title: Why his lactate kept climbing
science.text: Cells cut off from blood get no oxygen, so they fall back on glycolysis alone and turn the pyruvate into lactate. A rising lactate was his bowel reporting that it was running out of oxygen.

science.title: Why a twist stops blood both ways
science.text: Veins have thin walls and low pressure, so a twist closes them first. Blood can still get in but cannot get out. The loop swells until the pressure inside it stops the arteries too.

sources.title: Ten Broek et al. (World J Emerg Surg 2018): Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction
Maung et al. (J Trauma Acute Care Surg 2012): evaluation and management of small-bowel obstruction, an EAST practice management guideline

gs-058.title: Five days of fever _and shaking chills._

start.alarm: High fever · fast heart rate

gs-058.handoff: A 57-year-old man with diabetes was admitted today. He has had five days of high fevers with shaking chills and a dull pain under his right ribs. He was treated for a bowel infection two months ago.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fever and the pain
interview.finding: Five days of fevers up to 39 °C with shaking chills. He feels weak, has no appetite and has a dull pain under his right ribs. He has had night sweats and has lost 3 kg.

interview.prompt: Ask about travel, diarrhea and recent infections
interview.finding: He has not traveled abroad. No diarrhea and no blood in his stool. Two months ago he had diverticulitis, an infection of small pouches in the bowel wall, and was treated with antibiotic tablets.

interview.prompt: Ask about his diabetes and his medicines
interview.finding: His diabetes is poorly controlled, and he admits he often misses his tablets. He does not drink alcohol or inject drugs.

exam.prompt: Feel his liver, and tap over it
exam.finding: His liver is enlarged and tender. A light tap over his lower right ribs makes him wince.

exam.prompt: Look for yellow eyes, and press on the rest of his belly
exam.finding: The whites of his eyes are not yellow. The rest of his belly is soft.

exam.prompt: Listen to his chest, and check whether he is dry
exam.finding: Breath sounds are quiet at the bottom of his right lung, just above the liver. His heart is fast, and his mouth is dry.

1.label: Blood tests and CT scan
1.content:
White blood cells: 18.4, high.
Liver tests: raised, in the pattern seen when something inside the liver is blocking the flow of bile.
Blood sugar: 244, high.
Lactate: 2.1, borderline.
CT scan: a 6 cm pocket of fluid in the right side of the liver, divided into compartments, with a bright rim. A little fluid around the base of the right lung.
Blood cultures: sent, results pending.

0.resident: Fever, a tender liver and a high white count in a man with diabetes. I am worried there is an infection inside his liver.
0.question: Which test will show it?
options: A plain X-ray of his abdomen
A CT scan of his abdomen with contrast (or an ultrasound), and blood cultures
A camera test of his stomach (upper endoscopy)
A nuclear scan of his gallbladder (HIDA scan)
0.fix: Get the CT and blood cultures

terms.meaning: A walled-off pocket of pus.
Blood samples kept warm to see whether bacteria grow. They are taken before antibiotics, so the bacteria can still be found.
A dye given into a vein that makes blood vessels and inflamed tissue show up on a scan.

outcomes.story: You request a plain X-ray. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: An X-ray cannot see inside the liver. We need a scan that shows soft tissue.

outcomes.story: Blood cultures are drawn first. He goes for a CT scan, and the results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The scan shows the liver itself, and it will guide a drain if there is pus. Cultures first, so the antibiotics do not hide the bacteria.

outcomes.story: You request an endoscopy. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: That looks at the inside of the stomach. His problem is in the liver, which a camera in the stomach cannot see.

outcomes.story: The gallbladder scan takes two hours, and it is normal. While he lies in the scanner he has another shaking chill, and his blood pressure drops.
outcomes.reply: That scan only asks whether the gallbladder is blocked. His gallbladder was never the problem, and he has gone two more hours without a diagnosis. Get the CT now.

3.resident: He has a 6 cm pocket of pus in his liver, and the infection is spilling into his blood.
3.question: How do we treat it?
options: Antibiotics alone, with no drainage
Antibiotics through a vein, plus a drain placed through the skin under scan guidance
An emergency operation to remove that part of the liver
Metronidazole tablets alone
3.fix: Start antibiotics and call for a drain

terms.meaning: A thin tube passed through the skin into the abscess, guided by ultrasound or CT, to let the pus out.
Antibiotics that cover many kinds of bacteria, used until the lab names the one responsible.
The body’s dangerous, whole-body reaction to an infection.

outcomes.story: You write for antibiotics only. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: For a small abscess that can work. At 6 cm, antibiotics cannot get deep enough into the pus. It has to be drained as well.

outcomes.story: Antibiotics are started through a vein. A radiologist numbs the skin and slides a thin drain into the abscess under ultrasound. Thick pus comes out, and a sample goes to the lab. Within the hour his temperature starts to fall.
outcomes.reply: That is the treatment: antibiotics for the bacteria, and a drain for the pus. The sample will tell us which bacteria, so we can narrow the antibiotics.

outcomes.story: You ask about removing that part of his liver. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Surgery is kept for abscesses that a drain cannot empty. A needle and a tube do the same job with far less risk.

outcomes.story: You write for metronidazole tablets. The pharmacist calls.
outcomes.reply: Tablets of metronidazole alone treat an abscess caused by an ameba, a parasite. His is bacterial. He needs broader antibiotics through a vein, and a drain.
