4.resident: The lab has grown a single bacterium from the pus: Klebsiella pneumoniae. His fever is settling.
4.question: What else needs doing?
options: Look for where the infection came from, check his colon for a hidden cancer, and get his blood sugar under control
Nothing more
Start lifelong antifungal medicine
Order an ultrasound of his thyroid
4.fix: Plan the search for a source

terms.meaning: The place an infection started. Bacteria usually reach the liver from the bile ducts or from the bowel.
A camera test of the whole colon.

outcomes.story: You add a colonoscopy, a diabetes review and an eye check to his plan.
outcomes.reply: Good. Bacteria reach the liver from somewhere, often the bowel or the bile ducts. This particular bacterium, growing alone, has been linked to hidden colon cancer and to infection spreading to the eye.

outcomes.story: You say nothing more is needed. The resident disagrees.
outcomes.reply: An abscess has a source, and if we do not find it, it can come back. With this bacterium we also check the colon, and we fix his blood sugar.

outcomes.story: You suggest antifungal medicine. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: This is a bacterial infection, and antifungals do nothing for it. What he needs is a search for the source.

outcomes.story: You suggest a thyroid ultrasound. The resident looks puzzled.
outcomes.reply: His thyroid has nothing to do with a liver infection. Bacteria reach the liver from the bowel or the bile ducts, so that is where we look.

differential.resident: The blood tests and the scan are in his chart. Remember that he has not traveled.
differential.question: What is in his liver?
options: An abscess caused by an ameba, a parasite picked up abroad
An abscess caused by bacteria (pyogenic liver abscess)
A simple fluid-filled cyst
A hydatid cyst, from a tapeworm carried by sheep and dogs
differential.reveal: It is a bacterial abscess. Diabetes, a recent bowel infection, a high white count and a pocket with a bright rim and several compartments all fit. An amebic abscess needs travel to a place where the parasite is common. A simple cyst does not cause fever, and a hydatid cyst needs contact with livestock.

terms.meaning: Pus-forming. It means the cause is bacteria.
A bright ring on a contrast scan. It is the inflamed wall around a pocket of pus.

ending.stable: On the ward with a drain in his liver, and his fever coming down
ending.unstable: On the ward with a drain in his liver, and his fever coming down
ending.worse: On the ward with a drain in his liver, after a rougher day than he needed
ending.critical: In intensive care with sepsis

gs-058.plainDiagnosis: A pocket of pus in the liver caused by bacteria (pyogenic liver abscess).

science.title: Why he shook with cold while his temperature climbed
science.text: Infection raises the brain’s temperature set point. His body then treats 37 °C as too cold, so it shivers to make heat and narrows skin vessels to keep it. The chill is the body heating itself.

science.title: Why infection pushed his blood sugar up
science.text: Stress hormones released during infection tell the liver to put more glucose into the blood. Insulin normally answers that. With diabetes it cannot, so his sugar rose to 244, and high sugar in turn makes infection harder to clear.

sources.title: Lardière-Deguelte et al. (J Visc Surg 2015): hepatic abscess, diagnosis and management
Siu et al. (Lancet Infect Dis 2012): Klebsiella pneumoniae liver abscess, a new invasive syndrome

gs-052.title: Attacks of pounding headache, _a racing heart and sweat._

start.alarm: Blood pressure 176 over 104 on three medicines

gs-052.handoff: A 46-year-old man has had months of attacks: a pounding headache, a racing heart and drenching sweat, each lasting about 20 minutes. His blood pressure stays high on three medicines. A scan done for another reason found a lump on his right adrenal gland.

interview.prompt: Ask about the attacks
interview.finding: They last 15 to 30 minutes: a pounding headache at both temples, a racing heart, drenching sweat, shaking and a feeling that something terrible is about to happen. Bending over, exercise or straining can set one off. Between attacks he feels well.

interview.prompt: Ask about his blood pressure and his medicines
interview.finding: His doctors call his blood pressure hard to control. He takes three medicines for it. He has lost weight without trying and has become constipated.

interview.prompt: Ask about his family
interview.finding: An uncle had thyroid cancer. An aunt had tumors on both of her adrenal glands.

exam.prompt: Take his blood pressure lying down, then standing
exam.finding: 176 over 104 lying down. It falls to 150 over 92 when he stands, and his heart speeds up.

exam.prompt: Examine his heart and his belly
exam.finding: His heart is fast and regular, and it beats hard against the chest wall. His belly is soft, and no lump can be felt.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin, his neck and his eyes
exam.finding: His hands have a fine shake, and his skin is warm and damp. There are no unusual skin marks and no lump in his neck. The backs of his eyes look normal.

1.label: Hormone tests and CT scan
1.content:
Blood test for the breakdown products of adrenaline (metanephrines): about ten times the upper limit.
Urine collected over 24 hours: the same products, very high.
Cortisol test: normal.
Aldosterone test: normal. Potassium: normal.
CT scan: a 4.5 cm lump in the right adrenal gland. It is dense, not fatty, and patchy, and it is slow to clear contrast dye.

0.resident: Attacks like these, with a lump on the adrenal gland, make me think the lump is releasing bursts of adrenaline.
0.question: Which test checks that first?
options: A blood test for the breakdown products of adrenaline (plasma metanephrines)
A cortisol test after a dose of dexamethasone
A blood test of aldosterone and renin
A chromogranin A level alone

terms.meaning: A small gland on top of each kidney. It makes adrenaline, cortisol and aldosterone.
What adrenaline and noradrenaline are broken down into. A tumor leaks them all the time, even between attacks.

outcomes.story: Blood is drawn today, and he takes home a container to collect his urine for 24 hours. When he comes back, the results are in his chart with the rest of his adrenal tests.
outcomes.reply: Right. Adrenaline comes in bursts and is easy to miss. Its breakdown products leak out steadily, so the test catches the tumor even on a quiet day.

outcomes.story: You request the cortisol test. The resident adds another.
outcomes.reply: Worth doing for any adrenal lump, and we will. But too much cortisol does not cause attacks like his. Start with the test that fits the story.

outcomes.story: You request aldosterone and renin. The resident adds another.
outcomes.reply: Too much aldosterone causes steady high blood pressure with low potassium, not attacks of headache and sweating. We need the adrenaline test.

outcomes.story: You request chromogranin A. The resident changes it.
outcomes.reply: That marker goes up with many tumors and many other things. It cannot confirm this. The metanephrines can.

3.resident: It is a tumor that makes adrenaline, and it has to come out. But an operation on an unprepared patient can set off a flood of adrenaline.
3.question: What do we start first?
options: A beta-blocker, to slow his heart
An alpha-blocker for one to two weeks, with extra salt and fluids, and a beta-blocker only after that if it is needed
A calcium-channel blocker alone, and operate in 48 hours
An ACE inhibitor and a water tablet

terms.meaning: A medicine that stops adrenaline from squeezing the blood vessels. The vessels relax and the pressure falls.
A medicine that stops adrenaline from speeding the heart. It also blocks the small relaxing effect adrenaline has on some vessels.
A sudden, dangerous surge in blood pressure.

outcomes.story: He takes the first beta-blocker tablet in clinic. Within the hour his headache is blinding, he is pale and sweating, and his blood pressure has shot up.
outcomes.reply: This is why the order matters. With beta blocked, adrenaline can only squeeze his vessels, and nothing relaxes them. He needs an alpha-blocker now, and no more beta-blocker until that is working.

outcomes.story: An alpha-blocker is started, and he is told to eat salt freely and drink plenty. Over the next two weeks the dose is raised until his blood pressure is controlled. A beta-blocker is added only then, for his fast heart.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Alpha first, always. It relaxes vessels that adrenaline has kept squeezed for months, and the salt and fluid refill them. Then the surgery is safe.

outcomes.story: You suggest a calcium-channel blocker and surgery in two days. The surgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: Two days is not enough, and that medicine alone does not block adrenaline. He needs one to two weeks of an alpha-blocker before anyone operates.

outcomes.story: You suggest an ACE inhibitor and a water tablet. The resident points at his list.
outcomes.reply: He is already on both, and they have not worked. A water tablet also dries him out, when adrenaline has already shrunk the volume of his blood.

4.resident: Two weeks later you are in the operating room. His blood pressure is controlled, and the surgeon is about to remove the gland through keyhole cuts.
4.question: What keeps his blood pressure from surging during the operation?
options: Handling the tumor firmly from the start, to speed things up
Tying off the gland’s vein early, and handling the tumor as little as possible
Taking a biopsy first, to confirm what it is
Removing it without telling the anesthetist when

terms.meaning: The vein that carries the gland’s hormones into the bloodstream.
Taking a small sample of tissue with a needle.

outcomes.story: You suggest firm handling to save time. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Squeezing this tumor squeezes adrenaline into his blood. It is handled as little as possible.

outcomes.story: The surgeon clips the adrenal vein early, tells the anesthetist, then frees the gland gently and removes it. His blood pressure dips once the tumor is out, and fluids bring it back.
outcomes.reply: Right. Once the vein is closed, the tumor’s adrenaline has no route into the blood. The anesthetist needs warning, because the pressure can fall quickly when it comes out.

outcomes.story: You suggest a biopsy. The surgeon says never.
outcomes.reply: A needle into this tumor can release a flood of adrenaline or make it bleed. The blood tests and the scan already tell us what it is.

outcomes.story: You say the anesthetist does not need to know. The anesthetist looks over the drape.
outcomes.reply: They very much do. His pressure can spike while the tumor is handled and drop the moment it is out. They have to be ready for both.

5.resident: The tumor is out and he is recovering well. Remember his uncle’s thyroid cancer and his aunt’s adrenal tumors.
5.question: What should happen next?
options: Reassure him, with no more tests
Refer him for genetic counseling and testing, and check for the tumors that travel with this one
Start lifelong high-dose steroids
Remove his other adrenal gland now

terms.meaning: Passed down in a family through a gene.
An inherited condition that causes adrenal tumors, a type of thyroid cancer and overactive parathyroid glands.

outcomes.story: You say he needs nothing more. The resident disagrees.
outcomes.reply: Up to four in ten of these tumors run in families. With his family history, stopping here could miss a thyroid cancer in him or in his relatives.

outcomes.story: You book the genetics referral. The counselor will also offer testing to his relatives if a gene is found.
outcomes.reply: Good. If he carries one of these genes, we screen his thyroid and his other adrenal gland, and his family can be tested too.

outcomes.story: You suggest lifelong steroids. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: His other adrenal gland is healthy and makes all the cortisol he needs. He does not need replacement.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing the other gland. The surgeon says no.
outcomes.reply: There is no tumor in it. Taking it out would leave him dependent on steroid tablets for life, for nothing.

differential.resident: The hormone tests and the scan are in his chart.
differential.question: What is the lump?
options: A tumor making too much cortisol (Cushing syndrome)
A tumor making too much aldosterone (Conn syndrome)
A tumor making adrenaline-type hormones (pheochromocytoma)
A harmless fatty lump in the adrenal gland
differential.reveal: It is a pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland that releases adrenaline and noradrenaline in bursts. That explains the attacks and the stubborn blood pressure. His cortisol and aldosterone tests are normal, and a harmless lump would look fatty on the scan and clear the dye quickly.

terms.meaning: A tumor of the adrenal gland’s inner part that makes adrenaline-type hormones.
A sudden attack of symptoms that comes and goes.

ending.stable: Home after surgery with a normal blood pressure, and a genetics appointment booked
ending.worse: Home after surgery, after a blood pressure crisis in clinic that could have been avoided
ending.critical: In intensive care after a blood pressure crisis

gs-052.plainDiagnosis: An adrenal gland tumor that releases bursts of adrenaline (pheochromocytoma).

science.title: Why the tumor would not switch off
science.text: A healthy adrenal gland releases adrenaline only when nerves tell it to, and stops when the signal stops. The tumor ignores those signals and releases it whenever it is squeezed or stirred, which is why bending over could set off an attack.

science.title: Why adrenaline drives blood pressure up
science.text: Blood pressure depends on how hard the heart pumps and on how narrow the vessels are. Adrenaline-type hormones do both: they narrow the vessels through alpha receptors and drive the heart through beta receptors. Blocking alpha opens the vessels again.

sources.title: Lenders et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2014): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
Neumann, Young and Eng (N Engl J Med 2019): pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma

pd-027.title: Thirsty for weeks, _now hard to wake._

start.alarm: Breathing deep and fast · very sleepy

pd-027.handoff: A 9-year-old girl has been very thirsty and passing a lot of urine for three weeks, and she has lost weight. Since yesterday she has been vomiting. Today she is breathing fast and is hard to keep awake.

interview.prompt: Ask about the thirst, the urine and her weight
interview.finding: For several weeks she has been drinking and passing urine far more than usual, and she has started wetting the bed again after years of being dry. She has lost about 4 kg even though she eats well.

interview.prompt: Ask about the last day
interview.finding: Since yesterday she has felt sick, vomited and had belly pain all over. Today she is breathing fast and keeps falling asleep. Her parents say her breath smells like fruit or nail-polish remover.

interview.prompt: Ask about her health and her family
interview.finding: She has always been healthy and takes no medicines. She could not have swallowed anything harmful. She had a cold a few weeks ago. An aunt has type 1 diabetes.

exam.prompt: Watch her breathe, and smell her breath
exam.finding: Her breaths are deep and fast, as if she had just run a race. Her breath smells sweet and sharp.

exam.prompt: Check how dry she is
exam.finding: Her mouth is dry and her eyes are slightly sunken. Pinched skin is slow to flatten, and a pressed fingertip takes three seconds to turn pink again.

exam.prompt: Press on her belly, and check how alert she is
exam.finding: Her belly is tender all over, but it stays soft. She is sleepy and slow to answer, though she follows instructions. Her neck is not stiff.

1.label: Blood and urine tests
1.content:
Finger-prick blood sugar: 512, very high (normal is under about 140).
Blood acid level (pH): 7.18, acidic (normal is about 7.40). Bicarbonate, the blood’s main buffer: 9, very low.
Ketones in blood and urine: very high.
Potassium: 5.1, at the top of normal.
Kidney tests: mildly raised from dehydration.
HbA1c: 11.6%, which means her sugar has been high for weeks.
Urine: full of sugar and ketones, with no sign of infection.

0.resident: Weeks of thirst and weight loss, and now deep fast breathing with that smell on her breath. I think I know what this is, and a few quick tests will prove it.
0.question: What do we check first?
options: A CT scan of her head and a spinal tap, before anything else
A finger-prick blood sugar, a blood gas, blood salts and ketones
Thyroid and cortisol levels only
An ultrasound of her belly, for the pain
0.fix: Check her sugar, blood gas, salts and ketones

terms.meaning: A quick blood test that shows how acidic the blood is.
Acids the body makes when it burns fat because it cannot use sugar. They give the breath a fruity smell.

outcomes.story: She is taken for a head scan, which is normal. By the time she is back, 45 minutes have gone. She is harder to wake and is breathing even harder.
outcomes.reply: Her sleepiness comes from her blood chemistry, not from something a scan can see. A finger-prick would have told us in one minute. Do it now.

outcomes.story: The nurse pricks her finger while blood and urine are collected. The results are back within minutes and go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Sugar, acid, salts and ketones together make this diagnosis in minutes, at the bedside.

outcomes.story: You request thyroid and cortisol levels. The resident adds the tests she needs.
outcomes.reply: Those take hours and would not explain this. Her story points at sugar, so check the sugar.

outcomes.story: You request a belly ultrasound. The resident holds it.
outcomes.reply: Her belly hurts because her blood is acidic. An ultrasound would look normal and miss the emergency.

3.resident: She is dry, her blood is acidic and she has no insulin of her own. The order we fix things in matters a great deal in a child.
3.question: What is the right order?
options: A large dose of insulin into a vein at once, then fluids
Bicarbonate into a vein, to correct the acid quickly
Salt-water fluids into a vein first, check her potassium, then a slow, steady insulin drip
Drinks by mouth and insulin injections at home
3.fix: Start fluids, then the insulin drip

terms.meaning: The hormone that lets sugar move from the blood into cells. In type 1 diabetes the body stops making it.
Insulin given slowly and steadily into a vein, so sugar and acid come down gradually.
A blood salt the heart depends on. Insulin pushes it into cells, so the blood level can fall fast.

outcomes.story: You ask for a large dose of insulin straight away. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: Never in a child. A sudden dose shifts fluid and potassium too fast, and it raises the risk of brain swelling. Fluids first, then a slow drip.

outcomes.story: You ask for bicarbonate. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: It seems logical, and it makes children worse. Fluids and insulin stop the body making acid, and the blood then corrects itself.

outcomes.story: Fluids run for an hour, her potassium is confirmed and the insulin drip is started. Over the next few hours her sugar and her acid level improve. Then she says her head hurts badly. She is confused, her heart rate has dropped and her blood pressure has risen.
outcomes.reply: That was the right treatment in the right order. But something new is happening now, and it needs a name fast.
outcomes.alarm: Bad headache · confused · heart rate dropping

outcomes.story: You suggest treating her at home. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: She is too sick to drink, and her blood is dangerously acidic. She needs a drip and hourly checks in hospital.

4.resident: Four hours into treatment she has a bad headache and is confused. Her heart rate has fallen to 72, and her blood pressure has climbed.
4.question: What is happening?
options: Her brain is swelling (cerebral edema)
Her blood sugar has gone too low
A blood clot in her lung
Appendicitis
4.fix: Call it brain swelling and treat it

terms.meaning: Swelling of the brain. In a child being treated for ketoacidosis it is rare, and it is the complication doctors fear most.
Very salty fluid given into a vein. It draws water out of the swollen brain.

outcomes.story: You say it out loud. The team gives very salty fluid through her drip, raises the head of her bed and slows her other fluids. Within twenty minutes she is more awake and her heart rate recovers. She is moved to intensive care.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Headache, confusion, a slowing heart and a rising blood pressure during treatment mean brain swelling. It is treated on suspicion, without waiting for a scan.
outcomes.alarm: Treated for brain swelling · more awake

outcomes.story: You ask for a blood sugar. It is 240, nowhere near low. In the minutes that took she has stopped answering, and one pupil is larger than the other.
outcomes.reply: A low sugar causes shaking and sweating. It does not slow the heart and raise the blood pressure. This is her brain swelling, and she needs treatment this second.

outcomes.story: You suggest a clot in her lung. The resident points at the monitor.
outcomes.reply: A lung clot makes the heart race and the oxygen level fall. Her heart is slowing and her pressure is rising. That pattern means pressure in the skull.

outcomes.story: You suggest appendicitis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Her belly pain came from the acid and is already easing. A headache with confusion and a slowing heart points to her brain.

differential.resident: The blood and urine tests are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Very high blood sugar without acid in the blood (hyperosmolar state)
Diabetic ketoacidosis: high blood sugar, acid in the blood and ketones
Acid in the blood from a severe infection
Simple dehydration
differential.reveal: It is diabetic ketoacidosis, the first sign of type 1 diabetes in many children. Without insulin her cells cannot use sugar, so her body burns fat and makes acidic ketones. The three findings are all here: sugar of 512, acidic blood and large ketones. Her HbA1c shows this has been building for weeks.

terms.meaning: A condition in which the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin.
Blood that is more acidic than normal.

ending.stable: In the children’s intensive care unit, awake, on an insulin drip
ending.unstable: In the children’s intensive care unit, awake, on an insulin drip
ending.worse: In the children’s intensive care unit on an insulin drip, after a slow start
ending.critical: In the children’s intensive care unit, after her brain swelling went untreated for too long

pd-027.plainDiagnosis: A first attack of type 1 diabetes, with acid building up in the blood (diabetic ketoacidosis).

science.title: Why she was breathing so deep and fast
science.text: Ketones are acids, and they used up her bicarbonate buffer. Her body fought back the only fast way it can: by breathing out carbon dioxide, which pulls the buffer equation away from acid.

science.title: Why her body made ketones
science.text: Insulin is the signal that sugar is available. With none, her cells behaved as if she were starving: they broke down fat, and her liver turned it into ketones faster than she could use them.

science.title: Why her potassium was checked before insulin
science.text: Insulin switches on pumps that move potassium from the blood into cells. Her blood level looked normal, but her body was short of it. Starting insulin without checking could have dropped it far enough to disturb her heartbeat.

sources.title: Glaser et al. (Pediatr Diabetes 2022): ISPAD clinical practice consensus guidelines, diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state
Kuppermann et al. (N Engl J Med 2018): clinical trial of fluid infusion rates for pediatric diabetic ketoacidosis

pd-064.title: A five-day-old _vomiting bright green._

start.alarm: Green vomit · cool hands and feet · floppy

pd-064.handoff: A 5-day-old boy was feeding well until four hours ago, when he suddenly vomited bright green fluid. He has vomited three more times, will not feed and is becoming floppy and quiet.

interview.prompt: Ask his parents about the vomiting
interview.finding: It began suddenly four hours ago in the middle of a feed. The vomit is bright green. He has vomited three more times and now refuses the breast.

interview.prompt: Ask about his diapers and how he has been acting
interview.finding: He passed his first stool on day one and has had normal diapers since. Today’s diaper had a streak of dark blood. He was fussy and now has spells of being limp and quiet.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pregnancy and the birth
interview.finding: He was born on time after a healthy pregnancy with normal scans. He has had no fever. Nobody in the family has had bowel problems.

exam.prompt: Check his circulation, and whether he is dry
exam.finding: His hands and feet are cool. A pressed fingertip takes three to four seconds to turn pink again. His mouth is sticky, and the soft spot on his head is slightly sunken.

exam.prompt: Look at his belly and press on it
exam.finding: His belly is slightly swollen and tender all over. Few bowel sounds can be heard. The skin over it looks normal.

exam.prompt: Check his bottom and his muscle tone
exam.finding: His anus is normal, and there is a little dark blood there. He feels floppier than a newborn should and cries when handled.

2.label: Contrast X-ray study and blood tests
2.content:
Contrast study (dye is given down the stomach tube and followed on X-ray): the first part of the small bowel does not cross to the left side as it should, and the dye spirals downward like a corkscrew.
Plain X-ray: very little gas in the lower bowel.
Blood gas: acidic, with a lactate of 4.2, raised. Lactate builds up when tissue is starved of oxygen.
White blood cells: 18.5, high.

0.resident: Green vomit in a newborn. The color matters more than anything else in this story.
0.question: What do we assume until it is proven otherwise?
options: Normal spitting up (reflux)
A twisted bowel, which is a surgical emergency
A thickened stomach outlet (pyloric stenosis)
Overfeeding
0.fix: Treat it as a twisted bowel

terms.meaning: Vomit stained green by bile. Bile enters the gut just past the stomach, so green vomit means a blockage below that point.
A twist of the bowel around its own blood supply.

outcomes.story: You call it reflux. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Spit-up is milky, and the baby stays well. Green means the bowel is blocked below the stomach, and in a newborn that is an emergency until proven otherwise.

outcomes.story: You say it plainly, and the resident nods. The team moves fast.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. If his bowel has twisted, the whole of it can die within hours. Everything we do next is built around that possibility.

outcomes.story: You suggest pyloric stenosis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That causes forceful vomiting at three to six weeks of age, and the vomit is never green, because the blockage is above where bile enters.

outcomes.story: You suggest overfeeding. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Overfed babies spit up milk and stay pink and hungry. He is green-vomiting, cool and floppy.

1.resident: He needs an X-ray study with contrast, and it will take a few minutes to set up. He is cool, floppy and dry right now.
1.question: What do we do while it is arranged?
options: Give rehydration fluid by mouth and watch him
A tube into his stomach, a drip with a fluid bolus, nothing by mouth, and the children’s surgeon called now
Anti-sickness medicine, and home with advice about reflux
Erythromycin by mouth, to speed up his gut
1.fix: Stabilize him and call the surgeon

terms.meaning: A thin tube passed through the nose into the stomach to empty it.
A measured amount of fluid given quickly into a vein to support the circulation.
No feeds or drinks at all, to rest the gut and prepare for possible surgery.

outcomes.story: He is offered fluid by mouth and vomits it all back, green. An hour later his belly is more swollen, and he is limp and gray.
outcomes.reply: A blocked gut cannot take fluid from above, and he has gone another hour without a drip or a surgeon. Tube, drip, fluids, and call surgery now.
outcomes.alarm: Limp and gray · belly more swollen

outcomes.story: A tube is passed into his stomach and drains green fluid. A drip goes in, and fluid is pushed. His feeds are stopped. The children’s surgeon is on the way, and the contrast study is done at once. The results go in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Empty the stomach, refill his circulation, and get the surgeon moving before the pictures are even back.

outcomes.story: You write for anti-sickness medicine and a discharge. The attending stops it.
outcomes.reply: Sending home a newborn who vomits green could kill him. He stays, and he needs a surgeon.

outcomes.story: You write for erythromycin. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: Pushing a blocked gut to squeeze harder does not help, and it could do harm. He needs his stomach emptied and a drip.

4.resident: The contrast study shows his bowel twisted into a corkscrew, and his lactate is up. His gut is running out of blood.
4.question: What is the treatment?
options: An emergency operation to untwist the bowel and fix its position (Ladd procedure)
Rest the bowel, and examine his belly every few hours
An operation to open the stomach outlet (pyloromyotomy)
An air enema to push the bowel back
4.fix: Send him to the operating room

terms.meaning: The operation for this condition. The surgeon untwists the bowel, cuts the bands that hold it wrongly and lays it out so that it cannot twist again.
Too little blood reaching a tissue.

outcomes.story: The surgeon reviews the pictures and takes him straight to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Nothing but an operation untwists it, and every hour of twisting costs him bowel.

outcomes.story: He is admitted for bowel rest and checks every few hours. Three hours later his belly is tight and discolored, and he hardly responds when touched.
outcomes.reply: A twisted bowel does not untwist by resting. He has lost three hours of blood supply to his gut. He goes to the operating room now.
outcomes.alarm: Belly tight and discolored · barely responding

outcomes.story: You suggest the stomach-outlet operation. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That fixes pyloric stenosis, which this is not. His stomach outlet is fine. His bowel is twisted further down.

outcomes.story: You suggest an air enema. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That treats a different problem, where one piece of bowel slides inside the next. It cannot untwist a volvulus.

5.resident: The surgeon has untwisted his bowel and is checking how much of it will recover. His parents ask what happens if a long piece has to be removed.
5.question: What would they need to know?
options: He could be left with too little bowel to absorb food, and need feeding through a vein (short bowel syndrome)
He would need a permanent stoma bag and could never be fed
The bowel grows back completely within weeks
It would cause pyloric stenosis

terms.meaning: Too little small bowel left to absorb enough food and water.
Feeding through a vein, with a mix of sugar, protein, fat and vitamins.

outcomes.story: You explain it gently, and the resident fills in the details for his parents.
outcomes.reply: That is right. It is the reason speed mattered so much today: the more bowel that survives, the less likely he is to need it.

outcomes.story: You say he could never be fed. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: That is too bleak. Feeds are built up slowly as the remaining bowel adapts. The real risk is having too little bowel to absorb enough.

outcomes.story: You say the bowel grows back. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: Removed bowel does not grow back. What is left can adapt and absorb more over time, but if too little is left he needs feeding through a vein.

outcomes.story: You mention pyloric stenosis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The two are unrelated. The risk after losing a long piece of bowel is not being able to absorb enough food.

differential.resident: The contrast study and the blood tests are in his chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A first part of the bowel that never formed an opening (duodenal atresia)
A thickened stomach outlet (pyloric stenosis)
A bowel that is not anchored in its normal position and has twisted (malrotation with midgut volvulus)
A severe bowel inflammation of newborns (necrotizing enterocolitis)
differential.reveal: His bowel did not settle into its normal position before birth, so it hangs on a narrow stalk, and it has twisted around its own artery. The corkscrew of dye is the twist. A bowel with no opening causes vomiting from the first day and shows a different pattern, and pyloric stenosis never causes green vomit.

terms.meaning: A bowel that did not rotate and anchor into its normal position before birth.
Most of the small bowel and the first half of the colon, all fed by one artery.

ending.stable: In the newborn intensive care unit after surgery, with his bowel untwisted
ending.unstable: In the newborn intensive care unit after surgery, with his bowel untwisted
ending.worse: In the newborn intensive care unit after surgery, after losing time at the start
ending.critical: In the newborn intensive care unit after surgery, with part of his bowel removed

pd-064.plainDiagnosis: A bowel that was never anchored properly and twisted around its own blood supply (malrotation with midgut volvulus).

science.title: Why one twist threatens the whole gut
science.text: Nearly all of his small bowel is fed by a single artery that runs through the stalk it hangs from. A twist of that stalk closes the artery, the way a kink closes a garden hose, and everything beyond it loses its supply at once.

science.title: Why his blood turned acidic
science.text: Bowel without oxygen makes lactic acid. The acid used up the bicarbonate that keeps his blood near neutral, so his blood gas read acidic. It was an early signal that tissue was in trouble.

sources.title: Langer (Surg Clin North Am 2017): intestinal rotation abnormalities and midgut volvulus
Applegate (Pediatr Radiol 2009): evidence-based diagnosis of malrotation and volvulus

pd-081.title: Red spots and bruises _on a child who feels fine._

start.alarm: Red spots and bruises · playing happily

pd-081.handoff: A 4-year-old boy has come out in tiny red spots on his shins and several large bruises over the last two days. He had two short nosebleeds yesterday. He is playing happily in the waiting room.

interview.prompt: Ask his mother about the spots and bruises
interview.finding: Tiny red dots appeared on his shins two days ago, then large bruises on his chest, back and arms. He had not fallen or been hit. He had two short nosebleeds yesterday.

interview.prompt: Ask about recent illness and how he has been
interview.finding: He had a runny nose, a cough and a slight fever about two weeks ago, and it cleared up without treatment. He is eating, playing and sleeping normally. No fever, no bone pain and no weight loss.

interview.prompt: Ask about medicines and his family
interview.finding: He takes no medicines and has had no ibuprofen or aspirin. Nobody in the family bleeds easily or has had leukemia.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin and inside his mouth
exam.finding: Pinpoint red dots are scattered over both lower legs, and they do not fade when pressed. There are bruises up to 3 cm across on his chest, back, arms and legs. A little dried blood sits at one nostril. Nothing is bleeding inside his mouth.

exam.prompt: Feel for swollen glands, and for his liver and spleen
exam.finding: No swollen glands in his neck, armpits or groin. His liver and spleen are not enlarged.

exam.prompt: Check for paleness and bone pain, and watch him move
exam.finding: He is not pale or yellow. Pressing on his bones and joints does not hurt. He walks, talks and plays normally.

1.label: Blood count
1.content:
White blood cells: 7.8, normal, with a normal mix of cell types.
Hemoglobin: 12.6, normal.
Platelets: 11, very low (normal is 150 to 450).
Blood film under the microscope: very few platelets, and some of them large and young. Red and white cells look normal.
Clotting tests: normal.

0.resident: Spots and bruises like these mean his blood is not clotting well. Every parent in this room is thinking the same word: leukemia. One part of what you found argues strongly against it.
0.question: Which finding is most reassuring?
options: He had a cold two weeks ago
The red dots on his legs
He looks well, and he has no swollen glands, liver or spleen
He is 4 years old

terms.meaning: Pinpoint red dots in the skin, caused by tiny bleeds. They do not fade when pressed.
Small blood cells that plug holes in blood vessels and start clotting.
A cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow.

outcomes.story: You point to the recent cold. The resident says it helps, but only a little.
outcomes.reply: A cold often comes before the harmless cause, but a child with leukemia can catch a cold too. The stronger clue is on the exam.

outcomes.story: You point to the red dots. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: The dots only tell us his platelets are low. They look the same whatever the cause.

outcomes.story: You point out how well he looks and his normal exam. A blood count is sent, and the result goes in his chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. Leukemia fills the marrow and spills into the glands, liver and spleen, and the child looks ill. He looks well, and none of those are enlarged. The blood count will confirm it.

outcomes.story: You point to his age. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Four is a peak age for the harmless cause and for leukemia alike. His age does not separate them.

3.resident: His platelets are 11, which is very low. But all he has is skin bruising and two nosebleeds that stopped.
3.question: What do we do?
options: An urgent platelet transfusion
Remove his spleen
Watch and wait, with clear advice for his parents and no rough play
High-dose cyclophosphamide into a vein

terms.meaning: Checking a child regularly without giving treatment, because the condition usually clears up by itself.
Giving blood or part of blood, such as platelets, from a donor.
An organ in the upper left belly that filters blood. It is where most of his platelets are being destroyed.

outcomes.story: You ask for platelets. The blood doctor on the phone says no.
outcomes.reply: His immune system would destroy donated platelets within hours, just as it destroys his own. Transfusion is kept for life-threatening bleeding.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing his spleen. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is a last resort for the rare child still affected years later. Most children recover fully within weeks to months without any treatment.

outcomes.story: You sit down with his mother. No contact sports or climbing frames for now, no ibuprofen or aspirin, and a repeat blood count next week.
outcomes.reply: Yes. We treat the child, not the number. He is bleeding only into his skin, so watching is safer than any drug. If he had serious bleeding there are medicines that raise the count quickly.

outcomes.story: You suggest cyclophosphamide. The resident says no.
outcomes.reply: That is a strong drug that suppresses the immune system, with serious side effects. It has no place in a well child whose condition should clear up without treatment.

4.resident: His mother asks what she should watch for at home. One warning sign matters far more than the rest.
4.question: What should bring them straight to the emergency department?
options: A few new red dots on his legs
Headache, vomiting, or being drowsy or confused
A mild bruise after rough play
A short nosebleed that stops with pressure
4.fix: Warn about signs of bleeding in the head

terms.meaning: Bleeding inside the skull. It is rare in this condition, fewer than 1 in 100 children, and it is the one real danger.

outcomes.story: You mention new red dots. The resident adds something.
outcomes.reply: New dots are expected while his platelets are low and are not an emergency. The sign that matters is headache, vomiting or drowsiness.

outcomes.story: You tell his mother, and she repeats it back. She takes home a sheet with the clinic number.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. Those are signs of bleeding inside the head. It is rare, but it is the one thing that cannot wait.

outcomes.story: You mention bruising. The resident adds something.
outcomes.reply: Bruises are expected, and they are the reason for avoiding rough play. The emergency sign is headache, vomiting or drowsiness.

outcomes.story: You mention nosebleeds. The resident adds something.
outcomes.reply: A nosebleed that stops with pressure can be handled at home. One that will not stop needs a doctor. But the sign to act on at once is headache, vomiting or drowsiness.

differential.resident: The blood count is in his chart. Look at which cells are low and which are normal.
differential.question: What is this?
options: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP): his immune system is destroying his platelets
Acute leukemia
A clotting system being used up throughout the body (DIC)
Hemolytic uremic syndrome: destroyed red cells with kidney failure
differential.reveal: It is immune thrombocytopenia. After a viral infection, his immune system has started destroying his own platelets by mistake. Only the platelets are low. His red cells, white cells and clotting tests are normal, and the large young platelets show that his marrow is working hard to replace them. Leukemia would disturb the other cells too.

terms.meaning: A low platelet count.
The soft center of bones, where blood cells are made.

ending.stable: Home with his parents, with a blood count booked for next week
ending.worse: Admitted to the children’s ward
ending.critical: In the children’s intensive care unit

pd-081.plainDiagnosis: A low platelet count caused by the immune system, after a viral infection (immune thrombocytopenia).

science.title: Why the spots came out on his shins
science.text: Pressure in a column of fluid rises with depth. In a standing child the small vessels of the lower legs carry the highest pressure, so with too few platelets to plug tiny leaks, that is where blood escapes first.

science.title: Why one low number was reassuring
science.text: A marrow crowded by leukemia fails at everything it makes: red cells, white cells and platelets. His count showed one low line and two normal ones. That pattern fits platelets being destroyed after they are made, not a marrow that cannot make them.

sources.title: Neunert et al. (Blood Adv 2019): American Society of Hematology 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia
Provan et al. (Blood Adv 2019): updated international consensus report on the investigation and management of primary immune thrombocytopenia

ob-001.title: 34 weeks pregnant, _with a headache that will not lift._

start.alarm: Blood pressure 168 over 112 · headache · flashing lights

ob-001.handoff: A 31-year-old woman is 34 weeks pregnant. Her blood pressure at clinic today was very high. She has had a throbbing headache for two days and sees flashing lights.

interview.prompt: Ask about the headache and her vision
interview.finding: A throbbing headache across her forehead for two days. Acetaminophen does not touch it. Her vision blurs at times, and she sees flashing lights.

interview.prompt: Ask about swelling, belly pain and the baby’s movements
interview.finding: Her hands and face have swollen over the past week. She has no belly pain. The baby is moving normally.

interview.prompt: Ask about this pregnancy and her blood pressure before
interview.finding: This is her second pregnancy. The first was healthy. Her blood pressure was normal at her earlier visits. Her mother has high blood pressure.

exam.prompt: Take her blood pressure again, and look for swelling
exam.finding: 168 over 112, the same as before. Her lower legs hold a dent when pressed, and her face and eyelids are puffy.

exam.prompt: Tap her knee reflexes, and flex her ankles quickly
exam.finding: Her knees jerk much more briskly than normal. When each foot is pushed up quickly, it beats twice by itself. Both are signs that her nerves are irritable.

exam.prompt: Feel her belly, and listen to the baby
exam.finding: Her womb is the right size and soft. Pressing under her right ribs does not hurt. The baby’s heart rate is 140 and responds normally.

1.label: Blood tests, urine test and baby’s tracing
1.content:
Platelets: 188, normal.
Kidney test (creatinine): normal.
Liver tests: normal.
Test for broken-down red cells (LDH): normal.
Urine protein: 0.6, raised (normal is under 0.3). Her kidneys are leaking protein.
Baby’s heart tracing: normal, with no contractions.

0.resident: Blood pressure this high in late pregnancy, with a headache and flashing lights, can be the start of something dangerous for her and the baby.
0.question: What do we do first?
options: Reassure her and send her home, with a clinic visit in a week
Send blood and urine tests that look for organ damage, and put the baby on a monitor
Get a CT scan of her head before anything else
Give a blood pressure tablet and send her home once the number is normal
0.fix: Send the tests and monitor the baby

terms.meaning: A condition of late pregnancy with high blood pressure and signs that organs are under strain.
Protein in the urine. Healthy kidneys keep protein in the blood.
A belt on the belly that traces the baby’s heart rate and any contractions.

outcomes.story: You start her discharge papers. The resident takes them back.
outcomes.reply: With that blood pressure and those symptoms she could have a seizure or a stroke at home. She stays until we know what this is.

outcomes.story: Blood and urine are sent, and a monitor is strapped on to trace the baby’s heart. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The tests show whether her kidneys, liver and blood are being damaged, and the monitor shows how the baby is coping.

outcomes.story: She is taken for a head scan, which is normal. Forty-five minutes have passed with nothing done about her blood pressure. Her headache is worse, and the number has climbed.
outcomes.reply: Her symptoms already have an explanation, and it is not one a scan can see. The scan cost her time at a dangerous blood pressure. Send the blood and urine now.

outcomes.story: You suggest a tablet and home. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Lowering the number does not treat the disease. She needs tests, seizure protection and a plan for delivery, all in hospital.

3.resident: This is preeclampsia with severe features. The two immediate dangers are a stroke from the pressure, and a seizure.
3.question: What do we start now?
options: Labetalol into a vein for the blood pressure, and magnesium sulfate into a vein to prevent seizures
Methyldopa tablets alone, and follow her as an outpatient
Magnesium alone, holding blood pressure medicine until she passes 180 over 120
A water tablet and less to drink, to bring down the swelling

terms.meaning: A drip that calms irritable nerves and prevents the seizures of preeclampsia. It is not a blood pressure medicine.
Seizures caused by preeclampsia.
160 over 110 or higher in pregnancy. It needs treatment within the hour.

outcomes.story: Labetalol is given into a vein in small doses, and a magnesium drip is started. Her reflexes, her breathing and her urine output are checked every hour. Over half an hour her blood pressure comes down.
outcomes.reply: Both, and now. One protects her brain from the pressure, and the other protects it from seizures. Neither does the other’s job.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure coming down · magnesium running

outcomes.story: You write for methyldopa and a clinic visit. The resident stops the order.
outcomes.reply: That tablet takes days to work, and she has severe features. She cannot be an outpatient today.

outcomes.story: The magnesium runs, and no blood pressure medicine is given. Forty minutes later her pressure is higher still. Her headache is severe and her vision is blurring.
outcomes.reply: Magnesium prevents seizures. It does not lower blood pressure. At 160 over 110 we treat within the hour, because that is the pressure at which strokes happen. Give the labetalol.

outcomes.story: You write for a water tablet. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: The swelling is not the danger, and her blood vessels are already short of fluid. A water tablet would make that worse.

4.resident: Her pressure is controlled and the magnesium is running. The medicines hold the disease back. They do not cure it.
4.question: What is the plan for delivery?
options: Wait until 39 weeks, with weekly blood pressure checks
A cesarean right now, whatever the baby’s tracing shows
Steroids for the baby’s lungs, steady her, and then move toward delivery now instead of prolonging the pregnancy
Home on labetalol tablets, and continue to 37 weeks

terms.meaning: A steroid given to the mother before an early birth. It helps the baby’s lungs mature.
The only cure for preeclampsia, because the placenta drives the disease.

outcomes.story: You suggest waiting to 39 weeks. The obstetrician says no.
outcomes.reply: With severe features, every extra week risks a seizure, a stroke or the placenta failing. At 34 weeks the baby does well outside. We do not wait.

outcomes.story: You suggest an immediate cesarean. The obstetrician shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: She needs delivering, but not necessarily by surgery. The baby’s tracing is normal, so labor can be started and a vaginal birth is possible.

outcomes.story: The first steroid injection is given. The obstetrician explains the plan to her: she stays on the labor ward, and labor will be started once she is steady.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Delivery is the cure. The steroids give the baby’s lungs a head start, and at 34 weeks the balance favors delivering.

outcomes.story: You suggest home on tablets. The obstetrician says no.
outcomes.reply: Severe preeclampsia is never managed at home. It can turn into seizures or organ failure within hours.

differential.resident: Her blood tests, urine test and the baby’s tracing are in the chart.
differential.question: What is the diagnosis?
options: High blood pressure of pregnancy alone (gestational hypertension)
Long-standing high blood pressure (chronic hypertension)
Preeclampsia with severe features
HELLP syndrome: broken red cells, a strained liver and low platelets
differential.reveal: It is preeclampsia with severe features. Her blood pressure was normal earlier in pregnancy and is now very high, her kidneys are leaking protein, and she has a headache and flashing lights. Pressure that high, or those symptoms, is enough to call it severe. Her platelets, liver tests and red cells are normal, so it is not HELLP.

terms.meaning: Signs that preeclampsia is threatening the brain, liver, kidneys, blood or lungs.
The organ that feeds the baby. In preeclampsia it releases substances that damage the mother’s blood vessels.

ending.stable: On the labor ward with her blood pressure controlled, being prepared for delivery
ending.unstable: On the labor ward with her blood pressure controlled, being prepared for delivery
ending.worse: On the labor ward being prepared for delivery, after too long at a dangerous blood pressure
ending.critical: In intensive care after a seizure

ob-001.plainDiagnosis: A dangerous rise in blood pressure in late pregnancy that is straining her brain and kidneys (preeclampsia with severe features).

science.title: Why her blood pressure rose
science.text: Blood pressure depends on how hard the heart pumps and how narrow the small arteries are. In preeclampsia, substances from the placenta make those arteries tighten all over the body, so the same flow needs a much higher pressure.

science.title: Why magnesium quiets irritable nerves
science.text: A nerve fires when calcium flows in through channels in its membrane. Magnesium competes with calcium at those channels. With less calcium getting in, nerves fire less readily, which is why her brisk reflexes are used to judge the dose.

sources.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (Obstet Gynecol 2020): gestational hypertension and preeclampsia
Magpie Trial (Lancet 2002): do women with pre-eclampsia, and their babies, benefit from magnesium sulphate?

ob-010.title: Pregnant, in pain, _and the scan shows an empty womb._

start.alarm: Pain low on the right · positive pregnancy test

ob-010.handoff: A 26-year-old woman has had worsening pain low on the right side of her belly for three days, with light spotting. Her period is about three weeks late, and a home pregnancy test was positive.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and the bleeding
interview.finding: A sharp pain low on the right side for three days, coming and going and getting worse. Moving makes it worse. She has had light spotting. Today her right shoulder aches.

interview.prompt: Ask about her periods and this pregnancy
interview.finding: Her last period was about seven weeks ago, and a home test was positive. She has not seen anyone about this pregnancy yet. She has one child, born at term.

interview.prompt: Ask about past infections, operations and contraception
interview.finding: She was treated for a chlamydia infection of the pelvis two years ago, and she has had an operation for an ovarian cyst. She had a coil removed some months ago. She smokes half a pack a day.

exam.prompt: Press on her belly
exam.finding: It is soft. The lower right side is tender, and she tenses when it is pressed.

exam.prompt: Do an internal exam
exam.finding: The neck of the womb is closed, with a little dark blood. The right side is tender and feels full, and moving the neck of the womb hurts. The womb is smaller than it should be at seven weeks.

exam.prompt: Look for signs she is losing blood
exam.finding: She is a little pale, and her pulse is slightly fast. Her blood pressure is normal.

1.label: Blood tests and ultrasound
1.content:
Pregnancy hormone level (hCG): 3,200. At this level a pregnancy in the womb should be visible on a scan.
Internal ultrasound: the womb is empty. Beside the right ovary, and separate from it, is a 3 cm mass with a bright ring around it, sitting in the fallopian tube. A small amount of free fluid lies behind the womb.
Hemoglobin: 11.8, slightly low.
Blood group: O negative.

0.resident: Pain and bleeding in early pregnancy. Before anything else, we need to know where this pregnancy is.
0.question: Which two tests tell us?
options: A repeat urine pregnancy test and a plain X-ray of her belly
A blood test for the level of pregnancy hormone, and an internal ultrasound
A CT scan of her belly and pelvis, and a urine test
A CA-125 blood test and a cervical smear
0.fix: Send the hormone level and get the ultrasound

terms.meaning: The pregnancy hormone. Its level in the blood rises quickly in the first weeks.
An ultrasound probe placed in the vagina. It sits close to the womb and ovaries, so it sees an early pregnancy clearly.

outcomes.story: You ask for another urine test and an X-ray. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: We already know she is pregnant, and an X-ray cannot show an early pregnancy. We need to know where it is.

outcomes.story: Blood is sent, and the ultrasound is done at the bedside. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. The hormone level tells us whether a pregnancy should be visible yet, and the ultrasound shows whether it is in the womb.

outcomes.story: You ask for a CT scan. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: A CT gives radiation to an early pregnancy and is worse than ultrasound at finding one. Ultrasound is the test.

outcomes.story: You ask for a CA-125 and a smear. The resident cancels them.
outcomes.reply: Neither has anything to do with pain in early pregnancy. The question is where the pregnancy is.

3.resident: The pregnancy is in her right tube, and it has not burst. She is steady, the mass is small, there is no heartbeat in it, and her liver and kidney tests are normal.
3.question: How can this be treated?
options: An open operation now to remove her womb
Send her home with no follow-up
Methotrexate, because she meets the conditions for treatment with medicine
High-dose estrogen

terms.meaning: A pregnancy growing outside the womb, most often in a fallopian tube. It cannot survive, and it can burst the tube.
A medicine that stops fast-dividing cells from copying their DNA. One injection can end a small ectopic pregnancy without surgery.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing her womb. The gynecologist says no.
outcomes.reply: Her womb is healthy. Even when an ectopic needs surgery, the operation is keyhole surgery on the tube.

outcomes.story: You start a discharge with no follow-up. The gynecologist stops it.
outcomes.reply: An ectopic can burst without warning. Nobody with one goes home without a plan and blood tests to follow.

outcomes.story: The gynecologist agrees, and pharmacy prepares the dose. While she waits, she suddenly cries out with severe pain all over her belly. She turns pale and sweaty, and her blood pressure drops.
outcomes.reply: That was the right plan for a steady patient. She is not steady any more. Something has just changed.
outcomes.alarm: Sudden severe pain · blood pressure 80 over 48

outcomes.story: You suggest estrogen. The gynecologist says no.
outcomes.reply: Estrogen does nothing to an ectopic pregnancy. The choices are methotrexate or surgery.

4.resident: Sudden severe pain, a blood pressure of 80 over 48 and a heart rate of 130. The tube has burst, and she is bleeding into her belly.
4.question: What do we do this minute?
options: Go ahead with the methotrexate
Emergency surgery, with fluids and blood on the way
Watch her, and repeat the hormone level in 48 hours
Painkillers by mouth, and home

terms.meaning: The tube tearing open. The torn vessels bleed into the belly.
Too little blood left in the circulation to supply the organs.
An injection for mothers with an Rh-negative blood group. It stops them making antibodies that could harm a later baby.

outcomes.story: The injection is given. Methotrexate takes days to work, and it does nothing for bleeding. Fifteen minutes later she can no longer sit up, and she barely answers.
outcomes.reply: Medicine is only for a tube that has not burst. Hers has, and she is bleeding fast. She needs blood and a surgeon now.

outcomes.story: Two large drips go in, and blood is called for. The gynecologist takes her straight to the operating room, removes the torn tube and stops the bleeding. She is given anti-D because her blood group is Rh negative.
outcomes.reply: Yes. A burst ectopic is a surgical emergency. Fluids and blood keep her alive on the way, and only the operation stops the bleeding.
outcomes.alarm: In the operating room · bleeding stopped

outcomes.story: She is left on the monitor to be watched. Half an hour later she slumps over. Her blood pressure can barely be measured.
outcomes.reply: Waiting two days is for a steady patient with a small ectopic. She is bleeding to death in front of us. Surgery, now.

outcomes.story: You suggest painkillers and home. The attending steps between you and the door.
outcomes.reply: She is in shock from bleeding inside her belly. She goes to the operating room, not home.

differential.resident: The hormone level and the scan are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A normal early pregnancy that is still too small to see
An ectopic pregnancy: the pregnancy is growing outside the womb
A molar pregnancy
A harmless ovarian cyst of normal pregnancy
differential.reveal: It is an ectopic pregnancy in her right fallopian tube. At a hormone level of 3,200, a pregnancy in the womb should be visible, and her womb is empty. The ringed mass beside the ovary is the pregnancy. Her earlier pelvic infection and surgery scarred the tube, which is how a fertilized egg came to be stuck there.

terms.meaning: The tube that carries an egg from the ovary to the womb.
The hormone level above which an ultrasound should be able to see a pregnancy in the womb.

ending.stable: In the recovery room after emergency surgery, with the bleeding stopped
ending.unstable: In the recovery room after emergency surgery, with the bleeding stopped
ending.worse: In the recovery room after emergency surgery, having lost more blood than she needed to
ending.critical: In intensive care after emergency surgery and a large blood transfusion

ob-010.plainDiagnosis: A pregnancy growing in a fallopian tube, which then burst (ruptured ectopic pregnancy).

science.title: Why her shoulder ached
science.text: Blood in the belly irritates the diaphragm. The diaphragm’s sensory nerve enters the spinal cord at the same level as nerves from the shoulder, and the brain cannot tell the two apart. So it reports the pain as coming from the shoulder.

science.title: Why methotrexate can end an early pregnancy
science.text: Cells that divide must first copy their DNA, and that takes a supply of building blocks made with the help of folate. Methotrexate blocks that supply. The cells of an early pregnancy divide faster than almost any others, so they are hit hardest.

sources.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 193 (Obstet Gynecol 2018): tubal ectopic pregnancy
Barnhart (N Engl J Med 2009): ectopic pregnancy

ob-064.title: Sudden pain _that came out of nowhere._

start.alarm: Severe pain in waves · vomiting

ob-064.handoff: A 22-year-old woman was at the gym three hours ago when a severe pain started low on her right side. It comes in waves, and she has vomited twice.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain
interview.finding: It began all at once, three hours ago, in the middle of a workout. It is sharp and severe, low on the right, and it comes in waves that spread to her right side and groin. She feels sick and has vomited twice.

interview.prompt: Ask about her periods and sexual history
interview.finding: Her last period was two weeks ago and her cycle is regular. She has one partner, and they use condoms. She has no bleeding or discharge.

interview.prompt: Ask about fever, urine, bowels and her ovaries
interview.finding: No fever, no burning when she passes urine and no diarrhea. Months ago a scan done for another reason showed a cyst on her right ovary.

exam.prompt: Press on her belly
exam.finding: It is soft. The lower right side is very tender, and she tenses when it is pressed. Letting go quickly does not make it worse.

exam.prompt: Do an internal exam
exam.finding: The right side is very tender, and a swollen lump can be felt there. The neck of the womb looks normal, with no discharge. The left side does not hurt.

exam.prompt: Tap over her kidneys, and listen to her belly
exam.finding: Tapping over her kidneys does not hurt. Her bowel sounds are normal.

1.label: Pregnancy test, blood tests and ultrasound
1.content:
Pregnancy test: negative.
White blood cells: 11.6, slightly high. Hemoglobin: normal. Urine: normal.
Internal ultrasound: the right ovary is swollen to 6.5 cm, with a 5 cm cyst inside it. Its small egg sacs are pushed out to the edge.
Blood-flow scan (Doppler): almost no blood flowing into or out of the right ovary. The left ovary has normal flow.
A small amount of free fluid in the pelvis.

0.resident: Sudden one-sided pelvic pain in a young woman. There is one test we do before any scan, every time.
0.question: Which test comes first?
options: A CA-125 blood test
A pregnancy test
An ESR, a blood test for inflammation
A CT scan of her pelvis
0.fix: Send a pregnancy test, then scan

terms.meaning: The lowest part of the belly, which holds the womb, ovaries and bladder.
An ultrasound that shows whether blood is flowing through a vessel.

outcomes.story: You request a CA-125. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: That marker goes up with almost anything that irritates the belly, and it would not change what we do. Pregnancy test first.

outcomes.story: The pregnancy test is run in minutes, and she is taken for an ultrasound with a blood-flow scan. The results go in her chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. A pregnancy in the wrong place can kill, and it changes every decision. Once we know, the ultrasound can look at the ovary.

outcomes.story: You request an ESR. The resident cancels it.
outcomes.reply: It says only that something is inflamed, somewhere. It cannot guide an emergency. Pregnancy test first.

outcomes.story: You request a CT scan. The resident changes the order.
outcomes.reply: Not before a pregnancy test, and a CT is worse than ultrasound at looking at ovaries. It also gives radiation she does not need.

3.resident: Her right ovary is swollen and has almost no blood flowing through it. It has twisted on its own stalk.
3.question: What happens next?
options: Admit her, and repeat the ultrasound in 24 hours
Emergency keyhole surgery to untwist the ovary
Painkillers by mouth, and a gynecology appointment
Antibiotics into a vein, and reassess
3.fix: Call the gynecologist for emergency surgery

terms.meaning: Keyhole surgery: a camera and fine instruments passed through small cuts in the belly.
Untwisting. It lets blood flow into the ovary again.

outcomes.story: She is admitted to wait for a repeat scan. Six hours later the pain is constant, and she has a fever. The gynecologist who finally sees her is dismayed at how long the ovary has gone without blood.
outcomes.reply: An ovary with no blood supply is dying, and a second scan tells us nothing new. She has lost six hours. She goes to the operating room now.

outcomes.story: The gynecologist sees her at once, gives her pain relief and takes her to the operating room.
outcomes.reply: Yes. A twisted ovary is an emergency. The sooner it is untwisted, the better its chance of surviving.

outcomes.story: You start a discharge with painkillers. The attending stops it.
outcomes.reply: She would be going home with an ovary that has no blood supply. This needs surgery today.

outcomes.story: Antibiotics run in. Three hours later nothing has improved. Her pain is worse, and her heart rate is climbing.
outcomes.reply: This is not an infection. The ovary’s blood supply is twisted shut, and antibiotics cannot untwist it. Three hours have been lost. Call the gynecologist now.

4.resident: You are watching the keyhole surgery. The right ovary is twisted and dark blue, with a 5 cm cyst that looks harmless. She is 22.
4.question: What should the surgeon do?
options: Remove the ovary, because it looks dead
Untwist it, keep it and remove the cyst, even though it looks dark
Untwist it, and stitch both ovaries in place as a routine
Close up without doing anything, and plan an operation later
4.fix: Say the ovary should be kept

terms.meaning: Removing a cyst while leaving the rest of the ovary.
Removing an ovary.

outcomes.story: You suggest removing it. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: How an ovary looks is a poor guide to whether it will survive. Many dark ovaries recover once the blood returns. In a young woman we keep it unless it is plainly dead.

outcomes.story: The surgeon untwists the ovary, removes the cyst and leaves the ovary in place to recover.
outcomes.reply: Right. Untwist it and keep it. The cyst was the weight that made it turn, so that comes out.

outcomes.story: You suggest stitching both ovaries down. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: That is not routine. It is considered only if an ovary twists again, or if it is the only one she has.

outcomes.story: You suggest closing and coming back later. The surgeon shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Leaving it twisted means losing it. It has to be untwisted now.

differential.resident: The pregnancy test and the scan are in her chart.
differential.question: What is this?
options: A burst ectopic pregnancy
A twisted ovary (ovarian torsion)
Appendicitis
Pelvic inflammatory disease, an infection of the womb and tubes
differential.reveal: Her right ovary has twisted on the stalk that carries its blood supply. The cyst made it heavy enough to turn. The scan shows a swollen ovary with almost no blood flow. A negative pregnancy test rules out an ectopic, appendicitis would not change the ovary, and a pelvic infection causes pain on both sides, with discharge and fever.

terms.meaning: An organ twisting on its own stalk, which cuts off its blood supply.
A fluid-filled sac in the ovary. Most are harmless, but a large one can make the ovary twist.

ending.stable: Recovering after keyhole surgery, with her ovary untwisted and kept
ending.worse: Recovering after keyhole surgery. Her ovary went hours longer without blood than it needed to, and only time will show how well it recovers
ending.critical: In intensive care

ob-064.plainDiagnosis: An ovary twisted on its own blood supply (ovarian torsion).

science.title: How the scan saw that blood had stopped
science.text: Sound that bounces off something moving comes back at a slightly different pitch. A Doppler scan listens for that shift from moving red blood cells. From her right ovary there was almost none, which meant almost nothing was moving.
science.lessonTitle: Read a wave and a logarithmic level

science.title: Why a cyst makes an ovary twist
science.text: The ovary hangs from a stalk. A cyst adds weight away from that stalk, so a sudden movement, like a jump at the gym, produces a turning force. A heavier, more lopsided ovary needs less of a push to rotate.
science.lessonTitle: Choose a force or energy model

sources.title: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 783 (Obstet Gynecol 2019): adnexal torsion in adolescents
Huchon and Fauconnier (Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol 2010): adnexal torsion, a literature review

im-034.title: Weeks of feeling weak, _and now he cannot stand._

start.alarm: Blood pressure 84 over 52 · nearly collapsed

im-034.handoff: A 38-year-old man nearly collapsed today. He has been tired, dizzy and losing weight for weeks, and he has been vomiting for two days with a stomach bug. His blood pressure is very low.

interview.prompt: Ask how the last few weeks have been
interview.finding: Weeks of worsening tiredness, poor appetite and feeling sick. He gets dizzy when he stands. He has lost about 7 kg and craves salty food. Today he nearly passed out.

interview.prompt: Ask about recent illness and his skin
interview.finding: He has had a stomach bug for two days, with vomiting and belly pain. Over recent months his skin and old scars have turned darker. Friends say he looks tanned, in winter.

interview.prompt: Ask about his medical history and any steroids
interview.finding: He has an underactive thyroid caused by his immune system and takes thyroid tablets. He was recently told he has vitiligo. He has never taken steroids in any form. His sister has type 1 diabetes.

exam.prompt: Take his blood pressure lying down, then standing
exam.finding: 84 over 52 lying down. It falls to 70 over 44 when he stands, and his heart races. His mouth is dry.

exam.prompt: Look at his skin and inside his mouth
exam.finding: The creases of his palms, his knuckles and the inside of his cheeks are darkly pigmented. His forearms have pale patches with no pigment at all.

exam.prompt: Press on his belly, and check how alert he is
exam.finding: His belly is soft and mildly tender all over. He is drowsy but answers sensibly. His neck is not stiff.

1.label: Blood tests and heart tracing
1.content:
Sodium: 126, low. Potassium: 6.1, high.
Blood sugar: 62, low.
Kidney tests: raised, from dehydration.
Cortisol: 2.8, far too low for someone this ill.
ACTH, the pituitary signal that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol: very high.
Heart tracing (ECG): tall, pointed T waves, a sign that the high potassium is affecting the heart.

0.resident: Low blood pressure, darkened skin, salt craving, and an illness that tipped him over. I think his body cannot make cortisol. Blood for cortisol and ACTH is being drawn now.
0.question: What do we do while the results are pending?
options: Hold all steroids until a stimulation test confirms the diagnosis
Give salt-water fluids and hydrocortisone into a vein now
Start antibiotics and admit him for observation only
Give dexamethasone only once the morning cortisol is back

terms.meaning: A hormone from the adrenal glands. The body needs more of it during illness, to keep blood pressure and blood sugar up.
Cortisol given as a medicine.
Shock caused by too little cortisol. It can kill within hours, and it is easy to treat.

outcomes.story: The stimulation test is booked and no steroid is given. An hour later his blood pressure has fallen further, and he is hard to rouse.
outcomes.reply: The test can wait. He cannot. The blood we already drew will give us the diagnosis, and steroid given now does not spoil it. Give the hydrocortisone.
outcomes.alarm: Blood pressure 76 over 46 · hard to rouse

outcomes.story: Fluids run in fast, with sugar added, and hydrocortisone is given into a vein. Within minutes his blood pressure starts to come up. His results go in the chart.
outcomes.reply: Right. In a suspected adrenal crisis we treat first and confirm afterward. Waiting for proof is what kills people.

outcomes.story: Antibiotics are started, and he is admitted to be watched. Ninety minutes later his blood pressure is lower still, and he is confused.
outcomes.reply: Nothing here points to a bacterial infection, and watching him does not replace the hormone he is missing. He needs hydrocortisone and fluids now.

outcomes.story: You suggest waiting for a morning cortisol. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Morning is ten hours away, and he is in shock now. We have drawn the blood we need. Treat him.

3.resident: His potassium is 6.1, and his heart tracing shows it. The cause is the missing adrenal hormones and the dehydration.
3.question: How do we deal with the potassium?
options: Give calcium into a vein to protect his heart, and carry on with fluids and hydrocortisone, which bring the potassium down
Start emergency dialysis
Give a large dose of a potassium-binding powder, and recheck in 24 hours
Give a potassium-sparing water tablet, so he keeps more sodium

terms.meaning: A blood salt that sets the electrical state of heart cells. Too much can stop the heart.
Calcium given into a vein. It steadies the heart’s electrical activity within minutes, though it does not lower the potassium.

outcomes.story: Calcium is given slowly into a vein, and the pointed T waves settle. The fluids and hydrocortisone keep running, and a repeat potassium an hour later is already lower.
outcomes.reply: Yes. Calcium protects the heart now, and treating the cause does the rest. With the hormone replaced, his kidneys start getting rid of potassium again.

outcomes.story: You ask about dialysis. The resident shakes their head.
outcomes.reply: Dialysis is for potassium that will not come down any other way. His will fall with fluids and hydrocortisone. He needs calcium to cover his heart in the meantime.

outcomes.story: You write for the binding powder and a recheck tomorrow. The resident adds to the order.
outcomes.reply: The powder takes hours, and his heart tracing is already abnormal. Calcium first, and a recheck within the hour.

outcomes.story: You write for a potassium-sparing water tablet. The pharmacist calls at once.
outcomes.reply: That tablet makes the body hold on to potassium. It is the opposite of what he needs.

4.resident: He is steady now. His adrenal glands will not recover, so what he is taught before he leaves matters as much as today’s treatment.
4.question: What does he need for the long term?
options: Lifelong replacement of both adrenal hormones, with extra doses when he is ill and an emergency injection to carry
Cortisol replacement only
A two-week course of steroids that tapers off and stops
A strict no-salt diet
4.fix: Explain lifelong replacement and sick-day rules

terms.meaning: A tablet that replaces aldosterone, the adrenal hormone that makes the kidneys keep sodium.
Doubling or tripling the steroid dose during illness, the way healthy adrenal glands would raise cortisol.

outcomes.story: You go through it with him: two tablets for life, more when he is ill, an injection kit for emergencies and a medical alert bracelet.
outcomes.reply: Exactly. Both hormones are missing, so both are replaced. The sick-day rules are what stop him ending up here again.

outcomes.story: You suggest cortisol alone. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: His adrenal glands make no aldosterone either. Without it he keeps losing salt and holding potassium. He needs both.

outcomes.story: You suggest a short course that stops. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: A taper is for people coming off steroid tablets. His glands cannot make cortisol at all, so stopping would bring him straight back in crisis.

outcomes.story: You suggest avoiding salt. The resident corrects you.
outcomes.reply: He loses salt in his urine. He needs more of it than most people, not less.

differential.resident: His blood tests are in the chart. Look at the cortisol next to the ACTH.
differential.question: Where is the problem?
options: In the adrenal glands themselves (primary adrenal insufficiency, Addison disease)
In the pituitary gland, which is not signaling the adrenals
In the hypothalamus, which is not signaling the pituitary
Too much water-retaining hormone (SIADH)
differential.reveal: His adrenal glands have failed. The pituitary is shouting, with a very high ACTH, and the adrenals are not answering, so cortisol stays low. The high potassium shows that aldosterone is missing too, which only happens when the glands themselves are damaged. The darkened skin comes from the high ACTH. His thyroid disease and vitiligo point to his immune system as the cause.

terms.meaning: The pituitary hormone that tells the adrenal glands to make cortisol.
Caused by the immune system attacking the body’s own tissue.

ending.stable: Admitted to the ward on hydrocortisone, with his blood pressure recovering
ending.unstable: Admitted to the ward on hydrocortisone, with his blood pressure recovering
ending.worse: In intensive care, after too long in shock without hydrocortisone
ending.critical: In intensive care on life support

im-034.plainDiagnosis: Adrenal glands that have stopped making their hormones, tipped into shock by an illness (adrenal crisis from Addison disease).

science.title: Why his ACTH was so high
science.text: Cortisol normally switches off its own signal: when it rises, the pituitary makes less ACTH. With no cortisol coming back, nothing applied the brake. The molecule ACTH is cut from also yields a hormone that darkens skin, which explains his tan.

science.title: Why he craved salt
science.text: Aldosterone tells the last part of the kidney tubule to pull sodium back into the blood and push potassium out. Without it he lost sodium, and water with it, in his urine, and kept potassium. His body asked for the salt back.

sources.title: Bornstein et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2016): diagnosis and treatment of primary adrenal insufficiency, an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline
Rushworth, Torpy and Falhammar (N Engl J Med 2019): adrenal crisis
